0.title: The Sound Church: Titus and the Gospel-Ordered Life
0.overview:
Titus is the most compressed of the three Pastoral Epistles — three chapters of extraordinary density that move from theology to character to conduct without pausing. Paul writes to Titus, his Greek co-worker and 'true child in a common faith,' whom he has left on Crete with a single, sprawling assignment: 'put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town' (1:5). The churches of Crete are young, disorganized, and under pressure from teachers who combine Jewish speculative traditions with moral permissiveness. Titus's task is to build a church that looks like the gospel it proclaims.

Crete was one of the ancient world's most storied islands — home to a hundred cities, to the legendary palace of Knossos and the Minoan civilization, and to a reputation for unreliability so notorious it had become proverbial in antiquity. The Cretan philosopher Epimenides (c. 6th century BC) had declared that 'Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons,' a statement Paul quotes in 1:12 without embarrassment — cultural honesty is not racism, and the false teachers have confirmed the description. Paul and Titus had apparently visited Crete together at some point unrecorded in Acts (probably during the period between Paul's first and second Roman imprisonments), planted churches across the island, and then Paul left Titus to complete the work while he moved on.

The letter's organizing principle is the word 'sound' — hygiainō (healthy, health-giving). Sound doctrine (1:9; 2:1), sound faith (1:13; 2:2), sound speech (2:8) are the letter's repeated standard. The false teachers produce diseased teaching — teaching that makes people spiritually sick. Sound doctrine, by contrast, produces healthy congregations: older men of dignity, older women who form the younger, young people of self-control, slaves whose conduct adorns the gospel. The letter is a sustained argument that right belief and right living are inseparable — that the grace of God which saves also trains; that the gospel is not just good news about forgiveness but the power that produces a 'people for his own possession, eager for good works' (2:14).

Two Christological passages make Titus indispensable for preaching the full person of Christ. In 2:13 the Greek grammar (Sharp's Rule) identifies Jesus Christ as 'our great God and Savior' — one of the New Testament's most explicit affirmations of full deity. In 3:4–7 the paragraph on regeneration, justification, and Spirit-renewal is one of the most complete soteriological statements in Paul's letters, anchoring the call to godly conduct in the deepest possible theological foundation: God saved us not because of what we did but entirely by his own mercy, through the Spirit's renewing, so that we might become heirs of the hope of eternal life. The letter that sounds like a manual of church order is, at its root, a profound meditation on grace.

1.title: The Ordered Church: Elders, Sound Doctrine, and False Teachers
1.overview:
Paul left Titus on Crete to finish organising the young churches. Chapter 1 has three parts: a long greeting that grounds everything in the God who cannot lie (vv. 1–4); the qualifications of elders, who must be men of proven character able to teach and to refute (vv. 5–9); and a sharp word about false teachers, mostly from the circumcision party, who teach for money and whose lives contradict their talk (vv. 10–16).

The parts belong together. The elders are defined by the threat, and the false teachers are exposed by the standard. Truth, Paul insists, “accords with godliness” (v. 1); men who “profess to know God, but … deny him by their works” (v. 16) have failed the test.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul, God’s servant and Christ’s apostle, writes for the faith of God’s chosen people and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, in the hope of eternal life promised by God, who cannot lie, before time began, and now revealed through the preaching entrusted to Paul. He greets Titus, his true son in their shared faith, with grace and peace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The God Who Cannot Lie, Writing to Crete

Apseudes, the unlying God (v.2), is the first thing Paul says about God to an island proverbial for lying (v.12); and the eternal promise reaches anyone only through preaching entrusted to a man (v.3).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Titus was the uncircumcised test case at Jerusalem (Gal 2:1-3) and the man sent into the Corinthian crisis (2 Cor 7:6).

Now: Knowledge of the truth is recognised by the godliness it produces (v.1).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, for the sake of the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness, in hope of eternal life, which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began and at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching with which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Savior;

Meaning first. Titus 1 is about order in young churches threatened by false teachers. Paul opens with an unusually full greeting that sums up his ministry: he serves the faith of God’s chosen people and their knowledge of the truth that produces godliness, all resting on the hope of eternal life promised by the God who cannot lie (vv. 1–4). Then he explains why he left Titus in Crete: to finish setting the churches in order and to appoint elders in every town (v. 5). The elders must be above reproach in family life (v. 6) and character, not arrogant, hot-tempered, drunken, violent or greedy, but hospitable, self-controlled, upright and holy; and they must hold firmly to the trustworthy message so that they can teach sound doctrine and refute those who oppose it (vv. 7–9). This was urgent, because many rebellious talkers and deceivers, especially from the circumcision party, were upsetting whole households for money (vv. 10–11). Even a Cretan poet had said Cretans were liars, beasts and gluttons; so Titus must rebuke them sharply, so that they become sound in the faith and stop following Jewish myths and human rules (vv. 12–14). To the pure, all things are pure; but the false teachers, defiled in mind and conscience, claim to know God while denying him by their deeds (vv. 15–16). Over the whole chapter stands the first thing Paul says about God: he never lies.

The setting. Titus was a Greek convert and one of Paul’s trusted troubleshooters. Paul had taken him, uncircumcised, to Jerusalem as a test case for the gospel’s freedom (Galatians 2:1–5). He was sent to Corinth to deal with a crisis and to organise the collection (2 Corinthians 2:13; 7:6–15; 8:6, 16–23). After Paul’s release from his first Roman imprisonment, he and Titus evangelised Crete, and Paul left Titus there to organise the churches, writing this letter around AD 63–65. Later Titus went to Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10). Crete is a large island south of Greece. Cretans were present at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), so there may have been believers there before Paul arrived.

The longest opening. This is the longest opening sentence in any of Paul’s short letters, and the length is the point. Titus is going to face people on Crete who claim superior knowledge, and before a word of instruction Paul sets out, in three verses, where the truth actually comes from: from the eternal purpose of a God who cannot lie, revealed in history, and handed to a preacher.

Paul, a servant of God. “Servant” (doulos) means slave, bondservant. Only here does Paul call himself a servant of God; elsewhere he is a servant of Christ Jesus. The title places him in line with Moses, David and the prophets, the servants of the LORD (Joshua 1:2; Jeremiah 7:25). It is the lowest word in the Roman household and the highest title in Israel’s Scriptures, and Paul wears both meanings at once.

And an apostle of Jesus Christ. Servant expresses humility; apostle expresses authority. The combination, God’s slave and Christ’s apostle, appears nowhere else in Paul, and the pairing is deliberate in a letter that will call both Father and Son our Saviour within four verses.

For the sake of the faith of God’s elect. “For the sake of” (kata) means in accordance with, with a view to. Paul’s apostleship exists to bring God’s elect to faith and to build up their faith. “Elect” (eklektōn) means chosen ones. God chose a people; Paul preaches so that they will believe (2 Timothy 2:10; Acts 13:48). Election does not make preaching unnecessary; it guarantees its success.

Election comes first. God’s elect are those God has chosen for salvation, and Paul’s whole ministry serves their faith. Arminian Christians hold that God chose those he foresaw would believe. But Paul says the hope of eternal life was promised before the ages began (v. 2), and elsewhere that God saved us not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, given us in Christ Jesus before the ages began (2 Timothy 1:9). The more likely reading is that election comes first and faith is its fruit; and that is exactly why Paul preaches, so that the elect come to believe. The doctrine is not a reason to sit still. It is the reason a missionary can land on an island of liars and expect a church.

And their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness. “Knowledge” (epignōsis) means full knowledge, knowing that has taken hold. “Accords with godliness” (kat’ eusebeian) means leads to godliness, fits with it. There is the test that runs through all three of the letters to Timothy and Titus. Truth is recognised by the life it produces. A knowledge that leaves a man unchanged has failed the definition, whatever its content. True doctrine and godly life are inseparable, a theme of the whole letter (2:11–14; 3:8), and the false teachers on Crete had knowledge without godliness (v. 16).

In hope of eternal life. “Hope” (elpis) is confident expectation, not wishful thinking. Faith, knowledge and godliness all rest on the hope of eternal life (3:7). The Christian is not godly in order to earn a future; he is godly because a future has been promised to him and is certain.

Which God, who never lies, promised before the ages began. “Who never lies” (apseudēs) is a single word, the unlying God, and it occurs only here in the New Testament. Now recall where this letter is going. Crete, whose most famous literary export was the line Paul quotes in verse 12: Cretans are always liars. The first thing he says about God, in a letter to an island proverbial for deceit, is that he cannot lie (Numbers 23:19; Hebrews 6:18). Before the ages began (pro chronōn aiōniōn) is the same phrase as 2 Timothy 1:9. The promise was made before there was anyone to make it to. It was made in eternity, within the Trinity: the Father promised eternal life to the elect in Christ, before creation. This is sometimes called the covenant of redemption.

And at the proper time manifested in his word through the preaching. “At the proper time” (kairois idiois) means in his own seasons, as in 1 Timothy 2:6. “Manifested” (ephanerōsen) means made visible, revealed. “Preaching” (kērygma) means proclamation. The eternal purpose stayed hidden until an appointed moment, and then came out into the open. What God promised in eternity, he revealed in history through the preached gospel.

With which I have been entrusted by the command of God our Saviour. “Entrusted” (episteuthēn), as in 1 Timothy 1:11: the deposit word again. An eternal promise, revealed at the right hour, and then handed to a man to announce. That is how it reaches anybody, which is why appointing the right men in every town, in verse 5, is not administration but the survival of the thing. God our Saviour (1 Timothy 1:1) is a title used six times in this short letter, of the Father (1:3; 2:10; 3:4) and of Christ (1:4; 2:13; 3:6).

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul preached only to people he knew to be elect. He did not know who they were; he preached to all, knowing God would call his own through it. Nor does promised before the ages began mean anyone existed before time; it means God’s saving plan was fixed in eternity.

If God has chosen his elect, why should I share the gospel? Because God has chosen to save his elect through the gospel being shared. Election decides who will be saved; preaching is how they are reached. Paul endured everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation (2 Timothy 2:10). You do not know who the elect are, and you do not need to. Speak to everyone, pray for everyone, and trust God to open the hearts he has chosen to open, as he opened Lydia’s (Acts 16:14). Far from discouraging evangelism, election is its great encouragement: your words are not wasted, because God has a people and he will call them.

How can I know if I am one of God’s elect? Not by trying to look into God’s secret decrees, but by looking to Christ. The elect are those who come to Christ in faith, and whoever comes to him he will never cast out (John 6:37). If you trust Christ as your Saviour, love him, and want to follow him, that is the evidence that God chose you, because no one comes unless the Father draws him (John 6:44). If you are unsure, do not sit and wait to discover whether you are chosen; come to Christ now. Election is a doctrine for believers to rejoice in, not a barrier for seekers to stumble over.

In a sentence. From Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ, sent to bring God’s chosen people to faith and to the knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, all resting on the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began, and which at the time he chose he made known through the message entrusted to me by the command of God our Saviour.

On a Tuesday. Notice today the small untruths that are easy to tell: the excuse, the exaggeration, the flattering answer. You belong to the God who never lies. Let your yes be yes. And ask whether your knowledge of the truth is producing godliness, whether what you believe is changing how you live this week.

For worship. Praise the God who never lies. Before there was a world, a Cretan, or a single sinner, he made a promise in the counsel of the Trinity, and he has never once gone back on it. He kept it through the fall, the flood, the exile and four centuries of silence, and at the proper time he revealed it in his Son and sent preachers to announce it. Every promise he has made to you in Christ will be kept, because the one who made them cannot lie and cannot fail.
verseByVerse.note: Titus was a Greek convert and one of Paul’s trusted troubleshooters. The letter was probably written between Paul’s two Roman imprisonments, in the mid 60s AD.

verseByVerse.quote: To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To Titus, my true child in a common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.

To Titus, my true child. “True” (gnēsios) means genuine, legitimate, the real article, the same word used of Timothy (1 Timothy 1:2). Titus was probably converted through Paul. He is Paul’s authorised representative.

Who Titus was. He is a more formidable figure than his single short letter suggests. He was a Greek, and uncircumcised, and Paul took him to the Jerusalem council as a living test case, and records with some satisfaction that he was not forced to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1–3). Titus was the exhibit in the argument that settled whether Gentiles could be Christians without becoming Jews. He was also the man Paul sent into the worst of the Corinthian crisis, and whose return with good news comforted him (2 Corinthians 7:6, 13–15). Where Timothy is timid and needs steadying, Titus gets the hard postings. Paul has now left him on Crete.

In a common faith. “Common” (koinos) means shared, held in partnership. Paul the Jew and Titus the Gentile share one faith. There is not one faith for Jews and another for Gentiles, and the apostle and his delegate are not on different tiers of Christianity. They hold the same faith on the same terms. This was significant in a church troubled by the circumcision party (v. 10).

Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Saviour. Here Christ is called Saviour, just after the Father is called Saviour (v. 3). The same title is given to both. Watch it through the letter: God our Saviour, Christ our Saviour, alternating, six times in three chapters. The interchange is not careless. Christ is the Saviour along with the Father, which places him on the side of deity, and Paul will make the argument explicit at 2:13, where he calls him our great God and Saviour.

Textual note. Some later manuscripts add mercy, reading grace, mercy and peace, matching 1 and 2 Timothy. The earlier manuscripts have only grace and peace. Whatever the reason, the shorter greeting fits everything else we know: this is a letter to a man who does not need to be handled gently.

What it does not mean. Common does not mean ordinary or inferior; it means shared by all believers alike.

What does it mean to be someone’s child in the faith? It describes the bond between a believer and the person God used to bring him to Christ or to nurture him in his early years. It is a real family tie, and it carries love, gratitude and responsibility on both sides. It does not mean the spiritual father owns or controls the child; Titus is sent off to lead on his own. And you do not need to be an apostle to have one. A parent, a Sunday school teacher, a friend who explained the gospel, a pastor who walked with you: many believers have someone like that. Thank God for them, and ask him to let you be that for someone else.

In a sentence. To Titus, my genuine son in the faith we share: grace and peace from God the Father and from Christ Jesus our Saviour.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for a believer from a very different background who shares your faith. Tell them you are glad of them. And if someone first brought you the gospel, write to them this week and thank them.

For worship. Grace and peace come from two persons who are one God: the Father who planned our salvation and the Son who accomplished it, both rightly called our Saviour. They have made a Jew and a Greek into father and son, and joined Gentiles from every island and city into one household by one faith. There is no second-class place in it. Every believer holds the same faith on the same terms, because every believer has the same Saviour, and he gave himself for all of them alike.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–9 — Appointing Elders in Every Town
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul left Titus in Crete to finish organising the churches and appoint elders in every town. An elder must be above reproach, faithful in marriage, with believing children who are not wild or disobedient. As God’s steward an overseer must not be arrogant, quick-tempered, a drunkard, violent or greedy, but hospitable, a lover of good, sensible, just, holy and self-controlled. He must hold firmly to the trustworthy message as taught, so that he can encourage others with sound teaching and correct those who oppose it.
verseByVerse.theology:
Elder and Overseer Are One Office

‘Elders’ (v.5) and ‘overseer’ (v.7) name one office within a single sentence; and of the qualifications, eleven concern character and one competence — to instruct and to rebuke (v.9).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Congregations existed across Crete without yet being in working order (v.5).

Now: ‘Children are believers’ (v.6) — or ‘faithful’ — asks whether a household is visibly out of control, not whether a father has guaranteed his children's salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is why I left you in Crete, so that you might put what remained into order, and appoint elders in every town as I directed you— if anyone is above reproach, the husband of one wife, and his children are believers and not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination.

This is why I left you in Crete. Not abandoned: the verb describes a deliberate posting. Crete is a large island south of Greece. Acts records Paul only passing along its coast as a prisoner (Acts 27:7–13); the work there likely came after his release from his first imprisonment. Crete had about a hundred cities in ancient times, as Homer said; Paul and Titus had planted churches in several but had not finished organising them.

So that you might put what remained into order. “Put into order” (epidiorthōsē) means to set right further, to straighten out what remains. It is a medical word for setting a broken bone, or a carpenter’s word for straightening. What remained concedes that the work was unfinished. Paul is honest that he left a mess behind. The churches on Crete existed and were not yet in working condition. They were real but incomplete, and the chief need was proper leadership.

And appoint elders in every town. “Appoint” (katastēsēs) means to set in place, put in charge. “Elders” (presbyteroi) is plural: each town’s church was to have several elders. In every town: each local church needed its own leadership (Acts 14:23). Not one central church, but congregations scattered across an island. Paul’s answer to disorder is not a stronger central figure but properly constituted local leadership, which is why Titus’s job is to work himself out of one.

As I directed you. “Directed” (dietaxamēn) means arranged, gave orders. Paul had already given instructions verbally; he now puts them in writing for Titus’s authority, so that nobody on Crete could say Titus was acting on his own.

If anyone is above reproach. “Above reproach” (anenklētos) means unaccused, blameless, nothing outstanding that anyone can lay hold of, as with deacons in 1 Timothy 3:10. It is the headline qualification, repeated in verse 7, and the qualifications run closely parallel to 1 Timothy 3.

The husband of one wife. Literally a one-woman man: faithful in marriage, devoted to one woman (1 Timothy 3:2). The phrase speaks of faithfulness rather than issuing a ruling on every question of remarriage. Some read it as forbidding polygamy, others as forbidding any remarriage after divorce, others as requiring that elders be married. The more likely reading is that Paul asks for a man faithful to his wife. A single man is not excluded, since Paul himself was single. A man divorced long ago, or as the innocent party, may qualify if his life is now above reproach, and the church must judge each case with care. And the qualification assumes that elders are men, as in 1 Timothy 2:12 and 3:2: the office of elder belongs to qualified men.

And his children are believers. “Believers” (pista) can mean either believing or faithful, in the sense of trustworthy, well-behaved. Some think it requires that an elder’s children all be professing Christians; others that they be faithful, well-ordered and respectful. In 1 Timothy an overseer must keep his children submissive (1 Timothy 3:4); here the following phrase, not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination, suggests the emphasis is on their behaviour: children who are under his authority and are not wild or rebellious. This concerns children still at home.

And not open to the charge of debauchery or insubordination. “Debauchery” (asōtia) is wild, reckless living, dissipation; the word is used of the prodigal son’s reckless living (Luke 15:13). “Insubordination” (anypotaktos) means rebellious, unruly. If an elder cannot lead his own household, he cannot lead the church (1 Timothy 3:5). On a new mission field with a first generation of converts, the practical sense is plain: a man whose own household is visibly out of control is not the man to set a town’s church in order.

Where Christians differ: must an elder’s children be converted? Some insist that all an elder’s children must be professing Christians. Verdict: Since conversion is God’s work and not under a father’s control (John 1:13), and the word can mean faithful in the sense of trustworthy, it is better to read this as requiring that his children at home be orderly and respectful, not openly wild or rebellious, showing that he leads his household well. A father who has faithfully raised his children and whose child has not yet professed faith is not thereby disqualified, but a household in open disorder would disqualify him.

What it does not mean. It does not mean an elder must be married or have children; it describes how he must behave if he does. Nor does it require that adult children who have left home live in a certain way; the focus is the household under his authority.

Why does Paul care so much about an elder’s home? Because the home is where a man’s character is seen without a pulpit. Anyone can look godly for an hour on Sunday; his wife and children see him on Monday night. A man who is harsh, absent, or indifferent at home will be the same with the church, and a man who leads his family with patient, self-giving love is showing the very skills a church needs. That is why Paul puts the household first. It is also a reminder for every Christian husband and father, elder or not: your home is your first congregation, and the way you love your wife and children is the truest test of your faith.

If my child has walked away from the faith, have I failed? Not necessarily, and you should not carry a guilt God has not laid on you. No parent can give a child a new heart; that is God’s work (John 1:13). Faithful parents in Scripture had wayward children, and God himself, the perfect Father, had a rebellious son in Israel (Isaiah 1:2). Ask honestly whether there are ways you need to repent, and if so, confess them to God and, where it would help, to your child. Then keep praying, keep loving, keep the door open, and keep living the gospel in front of them. The prodigal’s father never stopped watching the road.

In a sentence. The reason I left you in Crete was so that you could put right what was still unfinished and appoint elders in each town as I instructed you. An elder must give no grounds for accusation, be faithful to his wife, and have children who are trustworthy and not open to the charge of wild living or rebellion.

On a Tuesday. Pray for your church’s elders and their families this week. Their homes are under pressure as well as their ministry, and the enemy knows that a pastor’s family is a target. Offer practical help: a meal, an evening of babysitting, an encouraging note to the elder’s wife.

For worship. Christ is the Chief Shepherd who sets his churches in order. He did not leave Crete to chance; he sent Titus with instructions, and he gives his church elders still, men who are themselves sheep under his care. And he is the perfect Husband of one bride, faithful to her without wavering, who will present her spotless; and the perfect Son, who did always what pleased his Father. Every faithful elder and every godly home is a small reflection of the household of God, where the Father rules in love and the Son serves to the end.
verseByVerse.note: Crete is a large island south of Greece. Acts records Paul only touching at it as a prisoner (Acts 27:7–13); this later work there is not in Acts.

verseByVerse.quote: For an overseer, as God's steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For an overseer, as God’s steward, must be above reproach. He must not be arrogant or quick-tempered or a drunkard or violent or greedy for gain, but hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught, so that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine and also to rebuke those who contradict it.

For an overseer. Paul now switches terms, elder in verse 5 and overseer (episkopos) here, and the switch is worth registering. The two words describe the same office, used interchangeably within two verses, in the middle of one sentence about one set of men. This is clear evidence that in the New Testament, elders and overseers (bishops) were the same people.

As God’s steward, must be above reproach. “Steward” (oikonomos) means household manager. In a large household the steward, very often a trusted slave, ran the estate on the owner’s behalf. He was a servant with authority, but accountable. The title carries real authority and no ownership whatever. He spends another man’s money and answers for it. The church is God’s household (1 Timothy 3:15); the elder manages it for God, not for himself.

He must not be arrogant. Then five things he must not be, and they read like a portrait of a bad manager. “Arrogant” (authadēs) is literally self-pleasing: self-willed, stubborn, insisting on his own way, the man who suits himself. A man who must always have his way cannot lead God’s household.

Or quick-tempered. “Quick-tempered” (orgilos) means prone to anger, irritable, the man with a short fuse.

Or a drunkard or violent. As in 1 Timothy 3:3. Violent means a striker, a man who hits people, whether with his fists or his words.

Or greedy for gain. “Greedy for gain” (aischrokerdēs) means fond of dishonest profit, as with deacons (1 Timothy 3:8). On Crete this was the live issue: the false teachers were in it for shameful gain (v. 11), and a man who wants money should not be given charge of a church’s.

But hospitable, a lover of good. Then six he must be. “Hospitable” (philoxenos) is literally a lover of strangers, and in a world without inns worth staying in, the church ran on it: travelling preachers, refugees, the poor, all needed a believer’s home. “Lover of good” (philagathos) means loving goodness, good people and good things, the opposite of those who in the last days will not love good (2 Timothy 3:3).

Self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined. “Self-controlled” (sōphrōn) means sensible, of sound mind. “Upright” (dikaios) means righteous, just in his dealings with people. “Holy” (hosios) means devout toward God. “Disciplined” (enkratēs) means self-mastered, in control of his desires: a man with a grip on himself.

Character first. Notice that all these items are about character, and then verse 9 gives the single competence. The list of what an elder is runs many times longer than the list of what he does, because the one skill demanded is inseparable from the man exercising it. On an island of empty talkers (v. 10), the difference between a true elder and a false teacher was never going to be fluency.

He must hold firm to the trustworthy word as taught. “Hold firm” (antechomai) means to cling to, to hold on against opposition. “Trustworthy word” (pistos logos) is the reliable message. “As taught” (kata tēn didachēn) means in accordance with the teaching: the apostolic doctrine as it was handed to him, rather than as he has developed it. An elder must be firmly committed to it, not wavering.

So that he may be able to give instruction in sound doctrine. “Give instruction” (parakalein) means to exhort, encourage. “Sound” (hygiainousa) means healthy, the word from which we get hygiene. Sound doctrine makes people spiritually well. This is his positive task: feeding the flock.

And also to rebuke those who contradict it. “Rebuke” (elenchein) means to refute, expose, convict. “Contradict” (antilegontas) means to speak against. This is his negative task: protecting the flock from wolves. Both are necessary, and the two halves must be kept together. Building up and pulling down. A man who can only encourage will watch the flock be eaten; a man who can only refute will do the eating himself. Paul requires both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean elders must be perfect. They are sinners saved by grace. It means their lives show mature, consistent godliness, and their doctrine is sound.

How should a church choose its elders? By looking for these qualities over time, not by electing the most successful, wealthy or outspoken men. Watch how a man treats his family, handles money, responds to criticism and serves when no one is looking. Ask whether he knows and loves the Bible and can explain it to others, and whether he can gently but firmly answer error. Give him time to be tested (1 Timothy 3:10; 5:22). Pray, as the church in Antioch did, before laying hands on anyone. And remember that the qualities are the same ones God wants in every believer; elders are simply men in whom they are mature enough to be an example.

What if my elders fall short of this list? Every elder falls short in some measure, and you should pray for them and bear with their weaknesses as they bear with yours. If a fault is minor, speak to them privately and kindly, or simply cover it with love (1 Peter 4:8). If it is serious and persistent, a pattern of anger, drunkenness, greed, harshness or false teaching, it should be raised with the other elders, with evidence, following 1 Timothy 5:19–20. An elder who is clearly disqualified should step down, and a church does him and itself no kindness by pretending otherwise. Never use the list as a weapon; use it as a standard everyone is glad to be held to.

In a sentence. Because an overseer manages God’s household, he must give no grounds for accusation. He must not be self-willed or short-tempered, given to drink, violent or out for dishonest money, but hospitable, a lover of what is good, sensible, fair, devout and self-disciplined. He must hold tightly to the reliable message as it has been taught, so that he can both encourage others with healthy teaching and refute those who oppose it.

On a Tuesday. Which of these qualities does God want to grow in you, whether or not you are a leader? Pick one and pray for it this week. If it is hospitality, invite someone into your home. If it is self-control, name the appetite that rules you and ask for help. If it is holding the word firmly, set aside time to learn one doctrine well.

For worship. Every quality in this list is found in perfection in one man. Christ is the Good Steward of his Father’s house, faithful over it as a Son. He was never self-willed, for he came not to do his own will. He was never quick-tempered, though slow to anger and abounding in steadfast love. He was never violent or greedy, but gave himself and his blood for his church. He welcomed strangers, loved what is good, was upright before men and holy before God, and held the Father’s word so firmly that he answered the devil with it. He feeds his flock with healthy teaching and drives off the wolves, and he will not lose one of his sheep.
verseByVerse.note: “Elder” (v. 5) and “overseer” here describe the same office.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Many in Crete, especially some Jewish Christians who insist on circumcision, are unruly talkers and deceivers who are upsetting whole families for the sake of money. Titus must silence them. Paul quotes a Cretan poet’s harsh verdict on his own people as liars and lazy gluttons and says it is accurate, so Titus must correct them firmly so that they become healthy in the faith and stop following Jewish myths and human rules. To the pure, everything is pure, but nothing is pure to those whose minds and consciences are corrupted. They claim to know God but their conduct denies him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Quoting a Pagan, and Agreeing With Him

Paul endorses Epimenides' verdict on Crete (vv.12–13) not as a racial claim but as the island's own accurate self-assessment — and rebukes sharply so that the offenders ‘may be sound in the faith’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Deceivers overturning whole households must be silenced (v.11), while the deceived are handled gently (2 Tim 2:25).

Now: ‘To the pure all things are pure’ (v.15) abolishes ritual defilement, not sin.

verseByVerse.quote: For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For there are many who are insubordinate, empty talkers and deceivers, especially those of the circumcision party. They must be silenced, since they are upsetting whole families by teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach.

For there are many who are insubordinate. The for ties this straight to the elder qualifications: this is why Titus needs men who can rebuke, and why sound elders were urgent. And many is not encouraging. The problem on Crete was not a fringe. “Insubordinate” (anypotaktoi) means rebellious, refusing to submit, unruly, refusing to be under anything: the same word used of an elder’s children in verse 6. They would not submit to apostolic authority.

Empty talkers and deceivers. “Empty talkers” (mataiologoi) are literally vain-speakers, idle talkers, speakers of nonsense, men whose words carry nothing (1 Timothy 1:6). “Deceivers” (phrenapatai) are mind-deceivers, seducers of the mind. The first describes the content, the second the effect: there is nothing in what they say, and it still leads people astray.

Especially those of the circumcision party. “Of the circumcision” (hoi ek tēs peritomēs) means Jewish Christians, or those influenced by them, who insisted on circumcision and the law of Moses, as in Galatia (Galatians 2:12; Acts 15:1, 5). There was a large Jewish community on Crete. Their teaching mixed Jewish myths, purity rules and speculation (v. 14; 3:9). Titus of all people knew what was at stake, having been the test case at Jerusalem (Galatians 2:3).

They must be silenced. Paul is unusually blunt. “Silenced” (epistomizein) means to stop the mouth, to muzzle; it is used of putting a bit in a horse’s mouth. Not engaged in endless dialogue. Stopped. Not by force, but by refuting them with sound doctrine (v. 9) and by refusing them a teaching platform in the church. That sits alongside the gentleness Paul commands elsewhere, correcting opponents with gentleness (2 Timothy 2:25), and the two are not in conflict once you see what he distinguishes. Gentleness governs how you treat the deceived. Silencing is for those doing the deceiving, when a congregation is being destroyed while the discussion continues.

Since they are upsetting whole families. “Upsetting” (anatrepousin) means overturning, as in 2 Timothy 2:18. “Whole families” (holous oikous) means entire households. The object is not individuals but households, which on Crete were the churches, since churches met in homes. False teaching could overturn a household’s faith and thus a whole house church at once.

By teaching for shameful gain what they ought not to teach. “Shameful gain” (aischrou kerdous) means dishonest profit. They taught for money (1 Timothy 6:5). There it is again, as in every one of these letters: money underneath the false teaching. And shameful is Paul’s own verdict on it, the same disqualification he had just listed for an elder in verse 7. The contrast is exact: the man who must not be greedy for gain, set against the men who teach for it.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Jewish believers were the problem as such; Paul himself was Jewish. The problem was teaching that added the law to Christ. Nor does silenced mean persecution or civil punishment; it means refutation and exclusion from teaching in the church.

How does a church silence false teachers today? By the means Paul gives, not by force. Elders who know the Bible answer the error clearly and publicly, so that the flock is not confused. False teachers are not given the pulpit, the Bible study, the youth group or the church newsletter. If a member persists in spreading serious error after patient correction, the church may have to remove him (3:10–11). Online, it means not sharing or promoting such teaching, and warning those in your care. None of this involves cruelty, slander or calling on the state to punish anyone. It is a shepherd closing the gate on the wolf.

Is it wrong for a teacher to be paid? No. Paul insists that those who labour in preaching and teaching deserve to be supported (1 Timothy 5:17–18). The sin here is teaching for shameful gain: shaping the message to make money, teaching what pleases the paying audience, or using religion as a business. The signs are not hard to spot: constant appeals for money, promises that giving will make you rich, a lifestyle far above the people who fund it, and no accountability. Support faithful teachers gladly. Be wary of anyone whose message always seems to end with your wallet.

In a sentence. There are many rebellious people, empty talkers and deceivers, especially among those who insist on circumcision. They must be stopped, because they are overturning entire households by teaching things they should not teach, for the sake of shameful profit.

On a Tuesday. Watch out for teachers who make money central. Support those who teach the gospel faithfully, and be wary of those who peddle it. And look at your own household: what voices are shaping the faith of your family, through screens, books and friends? Guard the door.

For worship. The Good Shepherd does not fleece his sheep. He gave his life for them. The false teachers on Crete came for what they could get; Christ came with nothing to gain and everything to give, and he still guards the households that belong to him. He has appointed shepherds to stop the mouths of wolves, and one day he will stop them all himself, when every empty word is silenced and his voice alone is heard.

verseByVerse.quote: One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons." This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,
verseByVerse.commentary:
One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sharply, that they may be sound in the faith,

One of the Cretans, a prophet of their own, said. Paul is quoting a pagan. The line is usually traced to Epimenides of Knossos, a Cretan poet-prophet of the sixth century BC, whom the Greeks regarded as a seer. Paul calls him a prophet in the sense the Cretans themselves used, not claiming that he was a true prophet of God. He does the same elsewhere, quoting Greek poets at Athens (Acts 17:28) and to the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 15:33).

Cretans are always liars. The reputation was real and proverbial. The Greeks had a verb, krētizein, to Cretanise, meaning to lie. One reason: Cretans claimed to have the tomb of Zeus, which to other Greeks was the founding Cretan falsehood, since they thought Zeus immortal. The contrast with God who never lies (v. 2) is pointed.

Evil beasts. “Evil beasts” (kaka thēria) means wild, dangerous animals: savage, brutal.

Lazy gluttons. Literally idle bellies (gasteres argai): people driven by their appetites and unwilling to work.

This testimony is true. Then Paul says it flatly. An apostle endorses a pagan poet’s description of his own people, in a letter of Scripture, and it needs care. Paul agrees that it describes the false teachers well: they lie, they are brutal in upsetting families, and they are driven by greed. Two things keep it from being what it looks like. First, Paul is not making a racial claim about Cretans as such. He has just left elders and congregations there, and Titus is to build them up. What he affirms is that the island’s own moral self-assessment was accurate, and that the false teachers he has just described are living down to it. A Cretan said this about Crete; Paul agrees that the cap fits the men in question.

Therefore rebuke them sharply. Second, note the purpose clause, because it changes everything. “Rebuke” (elenche) means refute, convict. “Sharply” (apotomōs) means severely, cuttingly, abruptly; the word is used of cutting off. The situation called for decisive correction, not gentle persuasion alone. A surgeon’s severity is not cruelty. Contrast 2 Timothy 2:25, where gentleness is urged; the method depends on the person and situation. The pastoral judgement underneath is that different people need different treatment. Timothy, timid, was told to be gentle and patient. Titus, on Crete, is told to cut. Paul has no single register, and a minister who only ever has one has not learned from him.

That they may be sound in the faith. “Sound” (hygiainōsin) means healthy. The sharpness has an aim, and the aim is their health. Sound is the medical word: Paul wants these people well. The goal of the sharp rebuke is restoration, not destruction. Them probably refers to the church members who were being influenced, and perhaps the false teachers themselves. A rebuke intended to make somebody healthy is a different act from a rebuke intended to put them in their place, even when the words are identical.

What it does not mean. It does not license ethnic stereotyping of people today. Paul is quoting a Cretan’s self-criticism to describe the false teachers’ character, and Paul’s own aim is that Cretans become sound in the faith; the gospel transforms every people. Nor does quoting a pagan poet mean his words are inspired; Paul’s use of them is inspired, as a true observation.

Is the saying self-refuting, since a Cretan said all Cretans are liars? Logicians have enjoyed the puzzle for centuries, but it is not what Paul is doing. It is a proverb about a people’s character, not a logical claim about every single Cretan on every occasion, and Paul agrees only with the observation it makes. Quoting a pagan writer’s true statement does not make him an inspired prophet, any more than quoting a newspaper makes it Scripture. All truth is God’s truth, and Paul is free to use it wherever he finds it.

How do I know when to rebuke sharply and when gently? Look at the person and the danger. Gentleness is right for the confused, the weak, the young believer who has stumbled, and anyone willing to listen (Galatians 6:1; 2 Timothy 2:24–25). Sharpness is right when someone is knowingly leading others astray, when gentle words have been ignored, or when great harm is being done and must be stopped at once. Even then, the aim must be the person’s health, never your own satisfaction. Check your motive: would you be glad if they repented and you never got the credit? Most of us lean naturally to one register; ask God to give you the other when it is needed.

In a sentence. One of their own, a Cretan whom they regarded as a prophet, said, “Cretans are always liars, savage beasts, idle bellies.” That description is accurate. So rebuke them severely, so that they may be healthy in the faith.

On a Tuesday. What sins is your culture known for? Ask God to make you different, and to use the gospel to transform your community. Be honest about the national or family failings you have inherited and are tempted to excuse because everyone around you shares them.

For worship. The gospel came to an island of liars, beasts and idle bellies and planted churches in it. That is the glory of God’s grace: he does not wait for a better people. He sent his Son to the Cretans, and to us, and makes liars into truthful men, savages into gentle ones, and the lazy into those zealous for good works. The God who cannot lie has spoken his word to a lying world, and it is changing the world one household at a time.
verseByVerse.note: The line is usually traced to Epimenides, a Cretan poet-prophet of about 600 BC.

verseByVerse.quote: not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
not devoting themselves to Jewish myths and the commands of people who turn away from the truth. To the pure, all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure; but both their minds and their consciences are defiled.

Not devoting themselves to Jewish myths. “Devoting themselves” (prosechontes) means paying attention to, as in 1 Timothy 1:4. “Jewish myths” (Ioudaikoi mythoi) are speculative stories and legends drawn from Jewish tradition, not Scripture itself. It is the same material as at Ephesus, myths and endless genealogies.

And the commands of people who turn away from the truth. “Commands of people” (entolai anthrōpōn) are human rules. Jesus condemned the same thing (Mark 7:7–8, quoting Isaiah 29:13). These were probably purity rules about food and ritual washing, as the next verse suggests (Colossians 2:20–23). Note the two halves: speculation on one side and man-made commands on the other. Fantasy and legalism, which look like opposites and regularly arrive together.

To the pure, all things are pure. Then verse 15, which is easily misused. The first half is a genuine principle and Paul means it. “Pure” (kathara) means clean. Purity is a matter of the heart, not of external rules. Against teachers imposing food laws and ritual restrictions, he says that for a person made clean by God, created things are clean. For those whose hearts have been cleansed by faith (Acts 15:9), no food or created thing is defiling in itself (Mark 7:15, 19; Romans 14:14, 20). It is the same argument as 1 Timothy 4:4, that everything created by God is good, and behind both stands the Lord’s own verdict, that nothing entering a man from outside defiles him.

But to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. The second half is the sharper observation. “Defiled” (memiammenois) means stained, polluted. “Unbelieving” (apistois). Defilement is not in the object but in the eye. To those whose hearts are unclean, everything they touch is defiled, because the defilement is in them. A corrupted mind manages to corrupt whatever it handles, including good and innocent things. And the reverse of the first principle is that such a man cannot be cleaned by rules about food, because the trouble is not in the food. Ritual rules cannot make them clean.

But both their minds and their consciences are defiled. “Minds” (nous) means thinking, reasoning. “Consciences” (syneidēsis) means moral awareness. Two faculties, and between them a man is finished. The mind judges what is true; the conscience judges what is right. When both are stained, there is no internal instrument left to detect the problem (1 Timothy 4:2), which is precisely why such men are confident, and why they must be silenced rather than reasoned with. Their thinking is twisted, and their moral compass is broken. The problem is not what they eat, but who they are.

What it does not mean. To the pure, all things are pure does not mean that nothing is sinful for a believer, or that a pure person can do anything. Paul is speaking of created things like food, not of sin. Sin remains sin. Nor does it mean a believer should ignore a weaker brother’s conscience (Romans 14:13–21). The verse abolishes ritual defilement; it does not abolish sin.

Does this mean I can watch or enjoy anything if my heart is pure? No. The verse is about created things that are good in themselves, food, drink, days, the material world, not about things that are sinful in their nature or that feed sin in us. Pornography, cruelty and blasphemy are not made clean by a believer watching them; and a pure heart is exactly the heart that does not want to be stained by them (Philippians 4:8). A Christian is free to enjoy God’s good gifts with thanksgiving. He is not free to call evil good. If you find yourself using this verse to justify something your conscience is uneasy about, that unease is worth listening to.

How do I get a clean conscience? Not by keeping more rules, but by the blood of Christ. Hebrews says the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:14). Bring your guilt to him by name and confess it; he is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse (1 John 1:9). Then believe what he says: you are clean. A conscience that keeps accusing you of forgiven sin needs to be taught by Scripture to rest in Christ’s finished work. And keep it clean by walking in the light, dealing with sin quickly instead of letting it build up. A conscience is a gift; treat it gently and keep it tender.

In a sentence. And will no longer pay attention to Jewish legends or to the rules of people who reject the truth. Everything is clean to those whose hearts are clean, but to those who are corrupted and do not believe, nothing is clean, because their very minds and consciences are polluted.

On a Tuesday. Are you more focused on external rules than on a clean heart? Ask God to cleanse your mind and conscience through Christ. Enjoy one of his good gifts today, a meal, a walk, a conversation, with conscious thanks, and refuse one thing you know would stain your mind.

For worship. The Lord who declared all foods clean also made unclean people clean. He touched lepers and was not defiled; he ate with sinners and was not stained; he went outside the camp to suffer, and by his blood he cleanses consciences from dead works. What no rule could do, his death has done. To his people the whole created world is given back as a gift, and the heart that was defiled is washed whiter than snow.

verseByVerse.quote: They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They profess to know God, but they deny him by their works. They are detestable, disobedient, unfit for any good work.

They profess to know God. It is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward, and it names the exact shape of the error. These men are not atheists and would be insulted to be called unbelievers. “Profess” (homologousin) means to confess, to claim openly. They make the claim, publicly and probably loudly, perhaps claiming special knowledge of God through their myths and rules.

But they deny him by their works. “Deny” (arnountai) means to disown, renounce. The two verbs are set against each other deliberately. Confession and denial are the great pair in the New Testament: whoever confesses me before men, and whoever denies me (Matthew 10:32–33). Paul says a man can perform the first with his mouth while performing the second with his life, and that the second is the one that counts. Their lives contradict their claims (2 Timothy 3:5; 1 John 2:4). What we do reveals what we really believe. The test of knowing God is obedience (Matthew 7:16–23; James 2:14–26).

The hardest person a church faces. This is the same figure as 2 Timothy 3:5, having the appearance of godliness but denying its power. These letters keep returning to him, because he is the hardest person a church has to deal with. An open opponent can be answered; a man whose profession is orthodox and whose life contradicts it cannot be, and he is usually inside.

They are detestable. Three words follow, and they escalate. “Detestable” (bdelyktoi) means abominable, disgusting. The word is related to the Old Testament term for an abomination to God, used in the Greek Old Testament of idols and unclean things. Ironically, they were obsessed with avoiding what was impure; yet they themselves were abominable. Men who talk endlessly about purity are pronounced unclean.

Disobedient. “Disobedient” (apeitheis) means refusing to be persuaded, rebellious: a different word from the insubordination of verse 10, but the same refusal to be ruled.

Unfit for any good work. “Unfit” (adokimoi) is the assayer’s term for metal tested and rejected: failing the test, disqualified, worthless, as in 2 Timothy 3:8. It closes the chapter on the note that opened it, a knowledge of the truth which accords with godliness (v. 1). Here is knowledge that accords with nothing. And good work (ergon agathon) introduces a theme of the whole letter: believers must be devoted to good works (2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14). The phrase comes again and again in three short chapters, and it starts here, with men who are fit for none.

What it does not mean. It does not mean good works save. Paul teaches clearly that we are saved not by works but by mercy (3:5). But true saving faith always produces good works (Ephesians 2:10). A profession of faith with no good works is empty. Paul is not about to argue that works save; he will say the opposite as plainly as it can be said. He is going to argue that grace produces them, and that a profession which produces none has already been tested and failed.

If I still sin a lot, am I denying God by my works? The fact that this question troubles you is a good sign. Paul is describing people whose lives as a whole contradict their profession, who are comfortable in disobedience and unfit for any good work, not believers who fight sin and often lose. Every Christian still sins (1 John 1:8), and the difference is not perfection but direction: do you hate your sin, confess it, and keep returning to Christ? Are there good works in your life, however small, that come from love for him? Then you are not the man in this verse. Keep looking to Christ, whose righteousness covers you, and whose Spirit is changing you.

What good works does God want from ordinary Christians? Mostly ordinary ones, done for his sake. Titus 2 and 3 will fill them in: loving your spouse and children, working honestly, being self-controlled, submitting to rightful authorities, being kind and gentle to everyone, helping those in urgent need, speaking evil of no one. Good works are not only religious activities; they are the whole of life lived in obedience and love. Ephesians 2:10 says God prepared them beforehand for us to walk in, so look for them in the place he has put you: your home, your street, your workplace, your church.

In a sentence. They claim to know God, but by the way they live they disown him. They are repulsive, rebellious, and no use for anything good.

On a Tuesday. Does your life confirm or contradict your profession of faith? Choose one good work to do this week that shows you know God: a debt paid, an apology made, a neighbour helped, a lonely person visited. Let your hands say what your mouth says on Sunday.

For worship. There was one man whose works and words never contradicted each other. Christ professed to know the Father and proved it by every deed; he could say, which of you convicts me of sin? He went about doing good, and then did the greatest good work of all, giving himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people zealous for good works (2:14). That is the answer to the hollow men of Crete. The Saviour who was approved in every test makes worthless metal into gold, and the people he saves become fit for every good work.
