2.title: Adorning the Doctrine: The Gospel-Shaped Community
2.overview:
Paul tells Titus how each group in the church should live: older men, older women, younger women, younger men, Titus himself, and slaves. Each instruction carries a missionary reason: so that God’s word is not slandered (v. 5), so that opponents have nothing bad to say (v. 8), so that slaves “adorn the doctrine of God our Savior” (v. 10). Ordinary conduct in ordinary roles makes the gospel look like what it is.

Then the reason underneath it all (vv. 11–14). The grace of God has appeared in Christ, and that same grace trains us to say no to ungodliness and to live well now, while we wait for the appearing of “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ”, who gave himself to redeem a people eager to do good. Grace saves, and grace trains.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — What Accords With Sound Doctrine
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Titus is to teach the way of life that matches healthy doctrine, group by group. Older men should be sober, serious, wise and sound in faith, love and perseverance. Older women should live reverently, avoid slander and drink, and teach what is good, especially to the younger women, encouraging them to love their husbands and children, live sensibly and purely, manage their homes, be kind and support their husbands, so that God’s word is not brought into disrepute. Young men should be self-controlled. Titus must model good works and serious, sound teaching that opponents cannot fault. Slaves should be dependable and honest with their masters, so that their lives make the teaching about God our Saviour attractive.
verseByVerse.theology:
Doctrine Has a Shape

Titus is to teach what accords with sound doctrine (v.1) — its natural clothing — and the climax is slaves adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour (v.10), the jewel shown to best advantage by the honesty of people with nothing to gain.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The only reason given for the household instructions is missionary: ‘that the word of God may not be reviled’ (v.5).

Now: Older women are commanded to teach (vv.3–4), which bypasses Titus entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. Older men are to be sober-minded, dignified, self-controlled, sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness.

Meaning first. Titus 2 shows what sound doctrine looks like when it is lived out in a church, and why. In contrast with the false teachers, whose lives denied God (1:16), Titus must teach what fits healthy doctrine (v. 1). Paul then goes through the household of faith group by group: older men are to be steady, dignified and sound in faith, love and endurance (v. 2); older women are to be reverent, not gossips or drinkers, and to teach what is good (v. 3), training younger women to love their husbands and children, to be sensible, pure, diligent at home, kind and submissive to their husbands, so that God’s word is not discredited (vv. 4–5); younger men are to be self-controlled, and Titus himself must model good works and teach with integrity (vv. 6–8); slaves are to serve faithfully and honestly so as to make the doctrine of God our Saviour attractive (vv. 9–10). Then comes the foundation of it all, one of the great gospel summaries in the New Testament (vv. 11–14): the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation, and it trains us to say no to ungodliness and to live godly lives now, while we wait for the blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ, who gave himself to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify a people for his own possession, eager to do good. Titus must teach these things with full authority (v. 15). The whole chapter moves between two appearings of Christ, and every ordinary duty in it is lit by both.

But as for you, teach what accords with sound doctrine. “But as for you” (sy de) marks the contrast with the empty talkers just described as unfit for any good work (1:10–16). Against them stands Titus, with a single instruction. “Teach” (lalei) means speak, keep speaking. “Accords with” (prepei) means is fitting, suitable, appropriate. “Sound doctrine” (hygiainousa didaskalia) is healthy teaching. Notice the phrasing, because it is doing something precise. Titus is not told only to teach sound doctrine, which he must obviously do, but to teach what fits it. The whole chapter is about behaviour, and Paul introduces it as the natural clothing of a body of truth.

Doctrine has a shape. That is the letter’s governing conviction. Doctrine has a shape, and a life either fits it or does not. Titus is not only to teach doctrine but also the way of life that fits it; doctrine and life go together. And it explains why what follows is so ordinary: no theology is expounded for ten verses, only how various people are to conduct themselves, because that is what accords with the theology. Then, when the theology comes in verses 11–14, it turns out to be the reason for every line.

Older men are to be sober-minded. Paul begins with the group most likely to think itself exempt. “Older men” (presbytai) means aged men, probably over fifty or sixty; not the office of elder, which is presbyteros. These are not officers; they are simply the older men in the congregation, and they get instructions like everybody else. “Sober-minded” (nēphalios) means temperate, clear-headed, as in 1 Timothy 3:2. Age can bring temptations to excess, complacency or bitterness; older men must stay alert.

Dignified. “Dignified” (semnos) means serious, worthy of respect. Their conduct should earn the respect their age deserves.

Self-controlled. “Self-controlled” (sōphrōn) means sensible, sound-minded, and it is a keyword of this chapter (vv. 2, 4, 5, 6, 12). It appears again and again, and it is plainly Paul’s central concern for Crete, an island known for its appetites.

Sound in faith, in love, and in steadfastness. “Sound” (hygiainontas) is the medical word, and here it attaches not to doctrine but to graces: healthy faith, healthy love, healthy endurance. Three virtues, like the familiar triad of faith, love and hope (1 Corinthians 13:13), but with steadfastness (hypomonē, patient endurance) in place of hope, since endurance is hope under pressure. And the third is the one that belongs particularly to age. Faith and love are asked of everyone; hypomonē, staying under the weight, is what a long life is uniquely placed to have learned and uniquely tempted to abandon at the end. Older men must not grow cynical in faith, cold in love, or weary in endurance.

A form of respect. There is a quiet dignity in this. Paul does not write old men off or reduce them to recipients of care. He gives them a standard to meet, which is a form of respect. The church still needs its older men, not only for their wisdom but for their example of finishing well.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only older men need these qualities; all believers do. Each group is given what it particularly needs. Nor does it suggest older people are past growing.

What are the particular dangers of growing old as a Christian? Scripture and experience suggest a few. Cynicism: having seen churches split and leaders fall, it is easy to stop expecting God to do anything. Coldness: love can shrink to a small circle of the familiar. Bitterness over losses and disappointments. Complacency: thinking the battle with sin is over. Self-indulgence, when duties are fewer. And weariness, the temptation to stop serving and let the young get on with it. Paul’s three words answer them: healthy faith that still trusts, healthy love that still reaches out, healthy endurance that keeps going. Moses was eighty when God called him, and Caleb at eighty-five asked for a mountain.

In a sentence. But you must teach what fits healthy doctrine. Older men should be clear-headed, worthy of respect and sensible, healthy in faith, in love and in endurance.

On a Tuesday. If you are older, ask God to keep you healthy in faith, love and endurance to the end, and look for one younger man you could encourage. If you are younger, thank an older believer for their example, and ask him what he has learned.

For worship. The God who gives these instructions is the Ancient of Days, whose years have no end, and who promises his people that even to old age and grey hairs he will carry them. He does not discard the old. He gives them work to do and grace to finish. And the Saviour they wait for endured to the end, setting his face to Jerusalem, and is able to keep every one of his people steadfast until the day they see him.

verseByVerse.quote: Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Older women likewise are to be reverent in behavior, not slanderers or slaves to much wine. They are to teach what is good,

Older women likewise are to be reverent in behaviour. Likewise: the same word, the same expectation. Paul is working through the congregation by age and sex, and nobody is left out. “Older women” (presbytides). “Reverent” (hieroprepēs) is a striking adjective: it is a temple word, meaning fitting for a temple, priest-like, holy in demeanour, as one carries oneself in a sacred place. Their whole bearing should be like that of someone serving in God’s presence. Paul is saying that an older Christian woman should move through ordinary life as though it were holy ground, which, given what he has just said about doctrine having a shape, it is. Their ordinary lives are worship.

Not slanderers. Then two things they are not to be, and they are startlingly specific. “Slanderers” (diaboloi) means accusers, malicious gossips, and it is the same term used of the devil himself: an accuser, a thrower-across (1 Timothy 3:11). That is a heavy word to use of gossip, and Paul uses it deliberately. A tongue that circulates accusations is doing recognisably the devil’s own work. Older women often know much about family and church life; they must not spread it.

Or slaves to much wine. The phrase is blunt and it names a real problem. “Slaves” (dedoulōmenas) is in the perfect tense: enslaved, in settled bondage. Drunkenness among older women was a known problem in the ancient world. Paul does not treat this as unmentionable or beneath discussion, and the candour is itself pastoral. Congregations that cannot name such things cannot help anyone caught in them. And these two are not a random pair. They are the characteristic temptations of people with time on their hands and less to occupy them than they once had, which is why the positive instruction follows immediately.

They are to teach what is good. One word in Greek, kalodidaskalous, teachers of good, and it occurs nowhere else in the Bible. Here is the answer to the two vices. An older woman with an empty diary will either fill it with wine and other people’s business or with this, and Paul assigns her a job. Older women have a vital teaching ministry. Not the public teaching office of elders (1 Timothy 2:12), but a powerful informal ministry, especially to younger women (v. 4), by word and example. And it should be said plainly what the passage shows. Paul restricted women from teaching authoritatively over men in the assembly, and here in the same breath he makes teaching a requirement for older women. Whatever the first passage means, it cannot mean women do not teach, because the man who wrote it commands them to.

What it does not mean. It does not limit older women’s teaching to these topics only; it highlights a key area. Nor does it mean women cannot teach anyone else; they rightly teach children (2 Timothy 1:5) and may explain the faith in many settings (Acts 18:26).

Does this mean Christians must not drink alcohol? No. The sin is being enslaved to wine, not using it. Scripture calls wine God’s gift to gladden the heart (Psalm 104:15), Jesus made it at a wedding (John 2:1–11), and Paul advised Timothy to take a little (1 Timothy 5:23). But Scripture also warns plainly against drunkenness (Ephesians 5:18), and some, for their own good or for the sake of others, will wisely choose not to drink at all. If you find that you need a drink, that you hide how much you take, or that others are worried, it may already have a hold on you. Tell someone, and get help; there is no shame in seeking freedom.

How can I tell the difference between sharing a concern and gossip? Ask who you are telling and why. Sharing is right when the person you tell can help, or needs to know for someone’s protection, and when you would be content for the person concerned to hear what you said. Gossip passes on another’s faults or troubles to people who cannot help, for the interest of the story, or to make yourself look better. A good test: have I spoken to the person first (Matthew 18:15)? Am I saying this in a way I would be willing to say it to their face? Would I want this said about me? When in doubt, pray about it instead of talking about it.

In a sentence. In the same way, older women should conduct themselves with a reverence fitting for those who serve God, not spreading slander or enslaved to drink. They should be teachers of what is good.

On a Tuesday. Older women: who is a younger woman you could mentor? Invite her for coffee this week, and ask how she is really doing. And if you notice a conversation turning to someone else’s business, gently turn it back.

For worship. The church is a temple, and every older woman who carries herself with reverence in ordinary life is showing that God lives there. The devil is the accuser; Christ is the advocate, who speaks for his people before the Father and never betrays a secret. He sets free those enslaved to wine and every other master, and gives them better work: to pass on what is good to those coming after. Thank God for the older women who taught you the faith.

verseByVerse.quote: and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.
verseByVerse.commentary:
and so train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, working at home, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, that the word of God may not be reviled.

And so train the young women. The content of that teaching is now specified, and this is the passage that gives modern readers most trouble. It repays reading exactly. “Train” (sōphronizōsin) means to teach to be sensible, to encourage, to bring to their senses, from the same root as self-controlled. Older women help younger women to think and live wisely. And note the mechanism Paul has set up: the older women teach the younger. Not Titus. He is the minister on the island, a young single man, and he would not be the best one to do this; the instruction hands the formation of young wives to older women who know what they are talking about.

To love their husbands and children. Two more single Greek words: philandrous, husband-loving, and philoteknous, child-loving, using the word for warm, affectionate love (phileō). And it is worth noticing that these are taught. Paul does not assume affection arrives automatically with marriage and motherhood, or that a woman struggling there is defective. Love in marriage and parenting does not always come naturally under the strains of daily life; it can and must be learned, from someone further along.

To be self-controlled, pure. “Self-controlled” (sōphrōn) means sensible. “Pure” (hagnos) means chaste, morally clean, sexually faithful.

Working at home. “Working at home” (oikourgous) means home-workers, busy at home; some manuscripts read oikourous, keepers of the home. It means managing the household diligently (1 Timothy 5:14; Proverbs 31:10–31), in contrast with the idle, gossiping younger widows of 1 Timothy 5:13. In the first century the household was a productive economic unit, weaving, food, managing servants and accounts, and a competent wife ran a small business. Proverbs 31 describes exactly such a woman, and she buys fields and trades. The word is about diligence and industry in the sphere she had.

Kind. “Kind” (agathos) means good, generous, benevolent. In a busy household with servants, children and guests, kindness is the quality that makes the home a refuge rather than a workplace.

And submissive to their own husbands. “Submissive” (hypotassomenas) means ordering themselves under, voluntarily yielding. It describes the wife’s voluntary, respectful following of her husband’s loving leadership (Ephesians 5:22–33; Colossians 3:18; 1 Peter 3:1–6). And the qualifier matters and is regularly dropped: their own husbands. Paul is not describing women as a class under men as a class; he is speaking of a marriage. And it stands within a New Testament frame that tells husbands to love their wives as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her (Ephesians 5:25), a demand which, if anything, costs more.

That the word of God may not be reviled. Then the reason, and it is the only one given here. “Reviled” (blasphēmētai) means slandered, blasphemed. If Christian wives abandoned their families or flouted their husbands, outsiders would blame the gospel. The purpose clause shows the evangelistic motive behind these instructions: making the gospel credible. Paul’s concern throughout is how the gospel looks to a watching pagan society. A movement whose converts were seen to wreck households would have been dismissed unheard, and he will not have the message discredited by the messengers’ domestic chaos.

Where Christians differ: does this teach a fixed role for wives in every culture? Egalitarians argue that Paul is accommodating to first-century culture to avoid offence, and that in a different culture, mutual submission without distinct roles would better adorn the gospel. Verdict: The motive is indeed partly missional (vv. 5, 8, 10). But elsewhere Paul grounds the wife’s submission in Christ’s relationship with the church (Ephesians 5:22–33) and in creation (1 Corinthians 11:8–9), which do not change with culture. This is the complementarian view: husbands and wives are equal in dignity and worth, with distinct and complementary roles. The husband leads with self-sacrificing love like Christ; the wife follows with respect and strength. This never means a wife must obey a command to sin (Acts 5:29), endure abuse, or lose her voice and gifts.

What it does not mean. It does not forbid women from working outside the home; the excellent wife of Proverbs 31 trades, buys land and sells goods. It means the home is not neglected. Nor does it make submission a matter of inferiority; Christ submitted to the Father, yet is equal with him (1 Corinthians 15:28). And it does not apply to single women, whose calling is equally honourable.

Must a wife submit to an abusive husband? No. Submission is given to a husband in his proper role, as to the Lord; it never means joining in sin, or enduring violence, threats or control. A husband who abuses his wife has abandoned the very headship he claims, which Scripture defines as giving himself up for her. A wife in danger should seek safety and help at once, and the church and the law should protect her (Romans 13:4). Leaders must never send her back into harm in the name of submission or reconciliation. Abuse may also be a form of desertion of the marriage covenant, and wise pastors will help her think through what Scripture allows. The church’s first duty is to the vulnerable.

What does submission look like in an ordinary Christian marriage? It looks like a wife who respects her husband, supports his leadership, speaks well of him, and is willing to follow his lead when, after honest discussion, they cannot agree on a decision. It does not mean she has no opinions, never disagrees, or does all the work; a wise husband seeks and values her counsel, as any good leader does. And it is matched by a husband who leads by serving: who takes responsibility, prays with his family, puts his wife’s good before his own, listens, and never uses his headship to get his own way. When both are walking with Christ, submission rarely feels like a burden; it feels like partnership with an order to it.

In a sentence. So that they can help the younger women learn to love their husbands and their children, to be sensible and pure, to work hard at home, to be kind, and to follow their own husbands’ lead, so that no one can speak against God’s word.

On a Tuesday. Wives: show your husband one specific act of love and respect this week. Husbands: lead in a way that makes that easy and joyful, by one specific act of sacrificial love. And if you are a younger woman, look for an older woman in your church you could learn from, and ask her.

For worship. Every Christian marriage is a small picture of a greater one. Christ is the Husband who loved his bride when she was unlovely, gave himself up for her, and is washing her clean. The church is the bride who gladly follows the one who died for her. When a Christian home is ordered in love, the watching world sees a glimpse of that, and the word of God is honoured. And single or married, every believer belongs to that marriage, and will sit at its supper.

verseByVerse.quote: Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works, and in your teaching show integrity, dignity, and sound speech that cannot be condemned, so that an opponent may be put to shame, having nothing evil to say about us.

Likewise, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. One instruction, and it is the same word again. “Urge” (parakalei) means exhort, encourage. “Self-controlled” (sōphronein) means to be sensible, to think soundly. Every group in this chapter gets it, but for young men it is the only thing said. The brevity is its own comment. Just one quality, but it covers everything: young men are prone to impulsiveness, anger, lust, pride and recklessness. Sound judgement and self-mastery are what they most need (2 Timothy 2:22).

Show yourself in all respects to be a model of good works. Then Titus himself, and the instruction turns personal. “Show yourself” (seauton parechomenos) means presenting yourself. Titus, probably himself a younger man, must teach younger men by example. “Model” (typos) is a die, a stamp, the pattern that shapes what is pressed against it, as in 1 Timothy 4:12. Titus is not merely to teach the chapter; he is to be the mould it is struck from. “Good works” (kala erga) is the theme of the letter once again.

And in your teaching show integrity. “Integrity” (aphthoria) means incorruption, purity, freedom from corrupt motives: teaching with no self-interest mixed in. Unlike the false teachers who taught for gain (1:11), Titus must teach with pure motives and unadulterated doctrine. On an island of men teaching for shameful gain, that was the visible difference.

Dignity. “Dignity” (semnotēs) means seriousness, gravity: treating the things of God with the seriousness they deserve. Not gloom, but weight.

And sound speech that cannot be condemned. “Sound speech” (logos hygiēs) is a healthy word. “Cannot be condemned” (akatagnōstos) means beyond criticism, unanswerable. His message should be so true and well-grounded that no fair critic can fault it. That does not mean speech nobody dislikes; it means speech that gives no legitimate handle.

So that an opponent may be put to shame. “Opponent” (ho ex enantias) is the one on the opposite side: false teachers or unbelieving critics. “Put to shame” (entrapē) means to be ashamed, embarrassed. When they look for something to attack and find nothing, they are left ashamed. Paul assumes there will be opponents; he does not aim at being liked. What he aims at is that when the opposition comes, it should have nothing true to work with. There is a great difference between a church that is attacked and a church that has handed its attackers the ammunition, and only the second is a disgrace.

Having nothing evil to say about us. Note the word us. Paul includes himself and all believers. What a young minister on Crete does with his teaching and his conduct will be laid at the door of the whole enterprise, the apostle included, which is a considerable weight to put on a man, and Paul puts it. A blameless life silences critics (1 Peter 2:12, 15).

What it does not mean. It does not mean critics will never attack; they will. It means our conduct should give them no legitimate grounds.

What does self-control look like for a young man today? It means mastering the appetites before they master you. Guarding your eyes and your screen against pornography, with accountability if you need it (Job 31:1). Controlling your temper, especially online and in traffic. Managing money instead of spending on impulse. Keeping your body under control in relationships with women, treating them as sisters in all purity (1 Timothy 5:2). Getting up in the morning and doing your work. Thinking before you speak. None of it is possible by willpower alone; it is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:23). But the Spirit works through your choices, so make them, and find an older man who will walk with you.

Do I have to be perfect before I can set an example? No. Titus was not perfect, and neither was Paul. A model of good works is someone whose life, taken as a whole, shows what following Christ looks like, including how to repent when you fail. Often the most helpful example a younger believer sees is an older one confessing a sin, apologising, and starting again. What disqualifies an example is hypocrisy: teaching one thing and living another without shame. So aim at consistency, not perfection. Let your life and your words point the same way, and when they do not, say so and put it right.

In a sentence. In the same way, encourage the younger men to be sensible. In everything set them an example by doing good; in your teaching show purity of motive, seriousness, and a healthy message that cannot be faulted, so that anyone who opposes us will be put to shame, having nothing bad to say about us.

On a Tuesday. Younger men: where do you most need self-control? Name it and ask a mature believer to hold you accountable. Everyone who teaches anything, in a class, a home, a workplace: ask whether your life would back up what you say, and close the gap where it does not.

For worship. Christ is the perfect pattern. He was a young man when he did his work, about thirty, and in all respects a model of good works; his teaching had integrity and dignity, and his enemies could find nothing to condemn, so that they had to hire false witnesses. He mastered every appetite in the wilderness, and he gives his Spirit of self-control to young men who cannot master themselves. Every faithful life that silences a critic is borrowing his.

verseByVerse.quote: Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything; they are to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not pilfering, but showing all good faith, so that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Savior.

Bondservants are to be submissive to their own masters in everything. The last group, and the largest in that world. “Bondservants” (douloi) means slaves. On slavery in the ancient world and Scripture’s response, see 1 Timothy 6:1–2. In everything means in all that does not require sin (Acts 5:29).

What Paul does and does not do. As at 1 Timothy 6:1–2, this must be read for what it does and does not do. Paul is not endorsing the institution. He lists enslavers among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10), tells masters they answer to a Master in heaven (Colossians 4:1), tells a slave to take freedom if he can get it (1 Corinthians 7:21), and sends a runaway back as a beloved brother (Philemon 16). What he is doing here is telling people with no legal power how to live with dignity inside a system they cannot change.

They are to be well-pleasing. Four instructions follow, and they are concrete. “Well-pleasing” (euarestos) means giving satisfaction: doing their work well.

Not argumentative. “Argumentative” (antilegontas) means talking back, contradicting, the constant low-level resistance of the powerless. It is the same word used of the false teachers who contradict the truth (1:9).

Not pilfering. “Pilfering” (nosphizomenous) means embezzling, secretly keeping back for oneself, the word used of Ananias keeping back part of the money (Acts 5:2–3). It means petty theft, helping yourself in small ways. Slaves often managed property, and petty theft was so common and expected that nobody thought it stealing. Paul does.

But showing all good faith. “Good faith” (pistis agathē) means complete trustworthiness, reliability. Taken together, the picture is a slave whose owner discovers that things stopped going missing and the back-answering stopped, and cannot account for it.

So that in everything they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour. Then the reason, and it is one of the most dignifying sentences in the New Testament. “Adorn” (kosmōsin) means to decorate, make attractive, arrange beautifully; it is the root behind our word cosmetic. It is used of setting jewels so that the stone shows to best advantage, or of jewels setting off a beautiful gown. Paul tells slaves, people with no legal standing, whose testimony was often not trusted in court, who could be beaten at will, that their honesty in small things displays the doctrine of God to its best advantage. The doctrine is already true; their lives display its beauty. No one is too lowly to adorn the gospel.

The setting for the jewel. Consider what that means for how the gospel commends itself. Not chiefly by argument or spectacle, but by the ordinary reliability of people with nothing to gain. The most powerless people in Crete are told they are the setting in which the jewel is shown, and everything in this chapter has been building to it: doctrine has a shape, and a life either fits it or does not.

What it does not mean. It does not endorse slavery as an institution. It tells believers in that hard situation how to live for Christ. The same principles apply to employees: honesty, diligence, respect and trustworthiness make the gospel attractive.

Why didn’t Paul simply condemn slavery? Because he was writing to a tiny, powerless minority with no means of abolishing it, and his aim in this letter is how believers should live where they are. But he planted the seeds that destroyed it. He taught that slave and master are brothers, equal in Christ (Galatians 3:28; Philemon 16), that masters must treat slaves justly and fairly because they too have a Master (Colossians 4:1), and that slave-trading is a sin against God’s law (1 Timothy 1:10). Where the gospel took hold, Christians in time came to see that the institution itself could not stand alongside it. Slavery as practised in the Atlantic trade, based on kidnapping and race, was condemned by Scripture from the start.

Does this mean I must obey my boss in everything? The principles apply to employees, with differences. You chose your job and can leave it; slaves could not. Within your work, be diligent, respectful, honest and reliable, even with a difficult manager (1 Peter 2:18). Do not talk back, take things home that are not yours, pad your hours or expenses, or quietly do less than you are paid for. But no employer has the right to require sin: falsifying records, deceiving customers, cutting corners on safety, or covering up wrongdoing. There you must obey God rather than men, respectfully, and accept the cost if it comes.

In a sentence. Slaves should submit to their own masters in everything, aiming to please them, not answering back, not stealing on the side, but showing that they can be fully trusted, so that in every way they make the teaching about God our Saviour attractive.

On a Tuesday. Can your employer trust you completely, with time, money and tasks? Let your work this week adorn the gospel. Find one small way you have been pilfering, minutes, stationery, a padded claim, and stop. Nobody may notice; God will, and so in time will the people who watch your life.

For worship. The doctrine these slaves adorned is the doctrine of God our Saviour, and he became a slave himself. The Son of God took the form of a servant, worked with his hands, washed feet, and was sold for the price of a slave. He did not answer back when he was reviled, and he kept nothing back for himself. Because he did, a Cretan slave could be told that his honest work in a kitchen made God beautiful to the watching world, and no believer since has been too lowly to do the same.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Behind all these instructions lies the gospel. God’s grace has come into view in Christ, offering salvation to people of every kind. That same grace teaches believers to say no to godlessness and worldly cravings and to live sensible, upright and devoted lives in the present age, while they wait for what they long for: the glorious appearing of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ. He gave himself to free us from all wrongdoing and to make us a cleansed people belonging to him, keen to do good. Titus is to teach these things with full authority and not let anyone dismiss him.
verseByVerse.theology:
Our Great God and Saviour Jesus Christ

By the construction Granville Sharp described, verse 13 names one person — Jesus Christ, our great God and Saviour — closing the letter's alternation of ‘God our Saviour’ and ‘Christ our Saviour’.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Grace appeared to all kinds of people — the slave on the same terms as the master (v.11).

Now: Grace is the schoolmaster (v.12), and a people eager for good works is what redemption produces, not its price (v.14).

verseByVerse.quote: For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people,

For the grace of God has appeared. For, and everything changes register. Ten verses of household instruction, and now Paul gives the reason underneath all of it. This is one of the great passages of the New Testament, and it exists to explain why an older woman should not gossip and a slave should not pilfer. Godly living is rooted in grace. “Grace” (charis) is undeserved favour. “Has appeared” (epephanē) is the shining-out word: used of the sun breaking through, like the sunrise from on high that visits us (Luke 1:78–79), and in that world of a god or a king making a public appearance. The word is related to epiphaneia, appearing. Grace was not merely announced or explained. It showed up, visibly, in a person: in Jesus Christ, in his birth, life, death and resurrection (2 Timothy 1:10; John 1:14, 17).

An event you could have attended. And the tense is aorist, past and definite. There was a point in history at which this occurred. Paul is not only describing a quality in God’s character, though it is that; he is describing an event you could have attended, in Bethlehem, in Galilee, outside Jerusalem.

Bringing salvation. “Bringing salvation” (sōtērios) means saving, salvation-bringing. Grace does not merely offer salvation; it brings it. It is not a possibility held out but a rescue carried in.

For all people. “For all people” (pasin anthrōpois). In context, all kinds of people: old and young, men and women, slaves and free (vv. 2–10). Paul has just addressed old men, old women, young women, young men and slaves. All people, in this chapter, means all kinds of people, and the grace that appeared is not restricted to any tier of society. Grace reaches even slaves, the lowest of society. That is the answer to a graded religion, and Crete had teachers offering one. On the island of the circumcision party, with its human commands and its inner knowledge, Paul says the grace of God has appeared to the slave in the kitchen on precisely the same terms as to the master.

Where Christians differ: does grace bring salvation to everyone without exception? Some read this verse as teaching that God’s grace makes salvation available to every individual equally, or even that all will be saved. Verdict: The context shows that all people refers to all kinds and classes of people listed in verses 2–10, as in 1 Timothy 2:4–6. Grace has appeared for every category of humanity, without distinction. And grace that brings salvation actually saves: it trains those it saves (v. 12) and it redeemed a particular people for God’s own possession (v. 14). This is consistent with definite atonement and effectual grace, while the gospel is still freely offered to everyone.

The order is never reversed. Note too the logic of the for. Paul does not say: behave well, and then grace may appear. He says behave well because it already has. The whole ethical section rests on a completed event, and that order is never reversed anywhere in Paul.

What it does not mean. It does not mean all people will be saved; Scripture teaches eternal judgement for those who reject Christ (Matthew 7:13–14; 25:46). Nor does it mean grace is merely an offer awaiting our decision; grace is God’s active, saving power.

If grace is for all kinds of people, can I tell anyone that Christ will save them? Yes, and you should. The gospel is to be offered freely and sincerely to every person, with the promise that whoever believes in Christ will be saved (John 3:16; Romans 10:13). You do not need to know whether someone is elect to tell them so; God has bound himself to save everyone who comes. There is no one whose background, class, race or past puts them beyond the reach of this grace: the slave and the master, the respectable and the notorious. Tell them that Christ receives sinners, and urge them to come.

In a sentence. For God’s grace has dawned on the world, bringing salvation within reach of every kind of person.

On a Tuesday. Think of the kind of person you find it hardest to imagine being saved, by class, background, politics or past, and remember that the grace of God has appeared for people like them. Pray for one of them by name today.

For worship. Thank God that his grace has appeared, not as an idea, but as a person: Jesus Christ, who came to save you. Grace was born in a stable, grew up in a carpenter’s house, touched lepers, ate with sinners, and was lifted up on a cross. It did not wait for us to rise to it; it came down to where we were and shone on the slave and the master alike. The sun of righteousness has risen with healing in his wings, and it will never set again.

verseByVerse.quote: training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,
verseByVerse.commentary:
training us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives in the present age,

Training us. “Training” (paideuousa) means educating, disciplining, instructing as a child is raised. It is the same root as the training in righteousness of 2 Timothy 3:16. And grace is the subject of the verb. That is the sentence’s astonishment. Grace is not only pardon; it is a teacher. The grace that saves us also trains us. The present tense makes it a lifelong school. The very thing people fear will make men careless is here the thing that trains them out of carelessness. Grace does not make us careless about sin; it makes us hate it.

Grace does the teaching. Anyone who has heard that too much emphasis on grace produces loose living should sit with this verse. Paul’s answer is not that grace must be balanced by law. It is that grace itself does the teaching, and does it better, because law can restrain conduct but cannot reach the wanting. A man who knows he is forgiven and loved at infinite cost does not want to go on wounding the one who loved him.

To renounce ungodliness. “Renounce” (arnēsamenoi) means to deny, to say no to, to reject decisively; it is the same verb used of Peter denying Christ. The aorist marks a decisive break, a definite refusal rather than a gradual cooling. “Ungodliness” (asebeia) is irreverence, lack of regard for God: the root sin, living as if God did not matter.

And worldly passions. “Worldly passions” (kosmikai epithymiai) are desires belonging to this world in its rebellion against God: lust, greed, pride, envy (1 John 2:15–17). Not desire as such, which God made, but desire bent toward what the world offers in place of him.

And to live self-controlled, upright, and godly lives. Then the positive, and it covers everything. Three adverbs, facing three directions. “Self-controlled” (sōphronōs), sensibly, the chapter’s word once more, facing inward toward oneself. “Upright” (dikaiōs), justly, righteously, facing outward toward others. “Godly” (eusebōs), reverently, devoutly, facing upward toward God. Between them there is no part of a life left over. A complete life.

In the present age. “Present age” (nyn aiōn) means this age now. Not in retreat from it, and not only in heaven, and not in some future condition when circumstances improve. On Crete, now, among the liars and the idle bellies. The grace that appeared in one age trains people to live in another one, and the training is for the age we are actually in. Grace equips us to live godly lives in an ungodly culture.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace makes effort unnecessary. Grace trains, and we learn; grace empowers, and we work (Philippians 2:12–13). Nor does it mean we will be perfect in this age; it means we will grow.

How does grace actually train me? Through the means God has appointed, used in the light of the cross. Grace teaches you through Scripture, which shows you what God loves and hates; through preaching, which applies it; through the Lord’s Supper, which sets Christ’s sacrifice before your eyes; through prayer, where you bring your struggles to him; through the church, where brothers and sisters encourage and correct you; and through providence, including hard things, which God uses to discipline his children for their good (Hebrews 12:10–11). And under all of it, grace trains by changing what you love. The more you see of Christ’s kindness, the less you want what he died to free you from.

What does saying no look like when temptation comes? It looks like a decision made in advance and acted on quickly. Know your particular weak points and plan for them: what you will not look at, where you will not go, what you will do instead. When the temptation comes, do not argue with it; turn from it, as Joseph ran (Genesis 39:12). Pray immediately, even one sentence. Remind yourself of the gospel: I am not a slave to this any more; Christ died to free me from it. Replace it with something good. And if you fall, do not wallow; confess it, receive forgiveness, and get up. Grace that says no to sin also says yes to the sinner who returns.

In a sentence. And it teaches us to say no to godlessness and the cravings of this world, and to live sensible, upright and devout lives in this present age.

On a Tuesday. What does grace need to train you to say no to this week? Ask God for the strength to say it, and the joy of living for him. Then pick one of the three directions, inward, outward, upward, and take one concrete step in it today.

For worship. The grace that trains us was itself trained. The Son learned obedience through what he suffered, said no to every worldly passion the devil offered him, and lived a perfectly self-controlled, upright and godly life in a present evil age. All of that righteousness is credited to us, and by his Spirit he now reproduces it in us. Grace is not a lenient master but a loving Father, who will not leave his children as he found them, and who never gives up on a pupil.

verseByVerse.quote: waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,
verseByVerse.commentary:
waiting for our blessed hope, the appearing of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,

Waiting for our blessed hope. The Christian life in this passage stands between two appearings. Grace appeared (v. 11); glory will appear (v. 13); and between them we live self-controlled lives in the present age. Everything in the chapter sits in that gap. “Waiting” (prosdechomenoi) means expecting, looking forward to, eagerly welcoming. It is not idleness. The present tense means continually waiting, and it is the same posture Paul commended when he said the crown goes to all who have loved his appearing (2 Timothy 4:8). “Blessed” (makaria) means happy, joyful. “Hope” (elpis) is not wishful thinking but certain expectation. Grace looks back to the first appearing and forward to the second, and between them we live godly lives (v. 12).

The appearing of the glory. “Appearing” (epiphaneia) is the word used for Christ’s return (1 Timothy 6:14; 2 Timothy 4:1, 8). “Of the glory” (tēs doxēs): not merely a glorious appearing, but the appearing of the glory itself, the visible display of divine splendour in Christ (Matthew 24:30; 25:31). The same word that described grace shining out in verse 11 now describes glory shining out. The first time, he came hidden in flesh; the next time, the glory will be unveiled.

Of our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. Now the crux, and it is one of the most important texts in the New Testament about who Christ is. The question is whether Paul is naming one person or two: our great God, and our Saviour Jesus Christ; or our great God and Saviour, who is Jesus Christ. In Greek, one article governs both nouns: tou megalou theou kai sōtēros hēmōn Iēsou Christou. By a well-known rule of Greek grammar, often called Granville Sharp’s rule, when one article governs two singular personal nouns joined by and, both refer to the same person. So Jesus Christ is both our great God and Saviour. Moreover, it is Christ, not the Father, whose appearing the New Testament expects. The same construction appears in 2 Peter 1:1. Other passages also call Jesus God (John 1:1, 18; 20:28; Romans 9:5; Hebrews 1:8).

The argument closes. And it explains the strange alternation running through this letter. Paul has said God our Saviour and Christ our Saviour, back and forth (1:3, 4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6). It looked careless. It was an argument being assembled, and here it closes. Which also lifts the chapter’s ordinary instructions into a startling light. The slave not pilfering in a Cretan kitchen is adorning the doctrine of God our Saviour (v. 10), and the God in question is the man who died for him.

Where Christians differ: is Jesus called God here? Some, including Jehovah’s Witnesses and some older scholars, translate the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, as referring to two persons, the Father and the Son. Verdict: The grammar, the context, and the New Testament’s consistent expectation of Christ’s (not the Father’s) appearing all support the translation our great God and Saviour Jesus Christ. This is the reading of most modern translations and of the early Greek church fathers, who spoke Greek as their native language. Christ is fully God, equal with the Father, one God in three persons.

What it does not mean. It does not mean the Father and the Son are the same person. They are distinct persons, both fully God. Nor does it mean Christ’s return is secret or partial; it is the public, visible, glorious appearing of God himself in the person of the Son, a single return at the end of the age.

Is our blessed hope a secret rapture before a tribulation? No. Paul names the hope directly: the appearing of the glory of our great God and Saviour. It is one glorious, visible appearing, and that is what believers wait for. Scripture describes Christ’s coming as public, like lightning across the sky (Matthew 24:27), with a shout and a trumpet (1 Thessalonians 4:16), when every eye will see him (Revelation 1:7). At that one coming the dead will be raised, believers will be gathered to meet him, the wicked will be judged, and all things made new. Christians will face trouble before then, as they always have, but their hope is not escape from the world; it is the return of its King.

How do I wait for Christ’s appearing in practice? By living now in a way that would be glad to be interrupted by him. Keep short accounts with God and with others. Hold your possessions loosely, since they will not last. Spend your life on what will: people, the gospel, good works. Pray for his coming, as the church has always prayed, come, Lord Jesus. Let the hope steady you in suffering, because the present age is not the last word. And do not waste energy on date-setting; he has told us to be ready, not to calculate. The best preparation for his appearing is the self-controlled, upright and godly life of verse 12.

In a sentence. As we wait for the joyful hope we look forward to: the appearing in glory of our great God and Saviour, Jesus Christ.

On a Tuesday. Ask yourself what you are most looking forward to this year, and whether Christ’s appearing is anywhere on the list. Then do one thing today that you would be glad for him to find you doing when he comes.

For worship. Worship Jesus Christ today as your great God and Saviour, and long for the day his glory appears. The baby of Bethlehem is the great God. The man who wept at Lazarus’s tomb is the great God. The one who hung on the cross, mocked and bleeding, is the great God and our Saviour. And he is coming again, not hidden this time but in the full blaze of the glory he had with the Father before the world existed. Every knee will bow. Those who have loved his appearing will see his face, and their waiting will turn to sight.
verseByVerse.note: One of the clearest New Testament statements that Jesus is God.

verseByVerse.quote: who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
who gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works. Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Let no one disregard you.

Who gave himself for us. The great God and Saviour of the previous verse is immediately described by a death. Paul does not let the highest statement of Christ’s deity stand for a sentence without the cross under it. “Gave himself” (edōken heauton) speaks of voluntary self-sacrifice (1 Timothy 2:6; Galatians 1:4; 2:20). And the giving is reflexive: he gave himself. Not something of his; not a contribution. The whole person handed over. “For us” (hyper hēmōn) means on our behalf, in our place. This is the heart of the gospel: substitution.

To redeem us from all lawlessness. Then two purposes, negative and positive. “Redeem” (lytrōsētai) means to ransom, to set free by paying a price. It is the language of buying a slave’s freedom (Mark 10:45; 1 Peter 1:18–19), and on Crete it would be heard by people who had watched it happen in a market, and by slaves in the congregation who longed for it. “All lawlessness” (pasa anomia) means every kind of sin, which is rebellion against God’s law (1 John 3:4), with nothing left unbought. Christ’s death frees us both from sin’s penalty (justification) and from its power (sanctification). Psalm 130:8 promised that God himself would redeem Israel from all its iniquities, and here the great God does it.

And to purify for himself a people. “Purify” (katharisē) means cleanse. Christ died not only to forgive but to make his people clean and holy (Ephesians 5:25–27; Hebrews 9:14). For himself: he is not cleaning them for someone else; he wants them.

For his own possession. “A people for his own possession” (laos periousios) means a special people, a treasured possession, and it echoes God’s words to Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; 14:2). Paul applies it, without apology, to a scatter of congregations on Crete containing slaves and former liars. What God said of the nation he brought out of Egypt he now says of them. The church, made of Jews and Gentiles, is God’s treasured people, the true Israel (1 Peter 2:9–10). Christ died with a particular people in view, whom he would redeem and make his own. This is definite atonement: his death actually secures the redemption and purification of those for whom he died.

Who are zealous for good works. “Zealous” (zēlōtēs) means eager, enthusiastic, passionate. The goal of redemption is a people burning with eagerness to do good. The chapter ends where the letter keeps ending. And note the order once more, because it is the whole architecture: he gave himself, he redeemed, he purified, he took possession, and the result is a people eager to do good. The works are not the price of the possession. They are what possession produces. Good works do not save, but those who are saved are zealous for them (Ephesians 2:10).

Declare these things; exhort and rebuke with all authority. Then verse 15, aimed squarely at Titus. “Declare” (lalei) means speak, as in verse 1. “Exhort” (parakalei) means encourage. “Rebuke” (elenche) means correct, convict. Announce, encourage, correct: all three are needed. “With all authority” (meta pasēs epitagēs) means with full command, the note of someone entitled to speak. Titus speaks with the authority of God’s word, not his own.

Let no one disregard you. “Disregard” (periphroneitō) means to think around, to look past, to look down on, despise. Timothy was told not to let anyone despise his youth (1 Timothy 4:12); Titus is told not to be ignored. Titus must not be intimidated, and the Cretans must not ignore him. And the instruction is oddly framed, because Titus cannot control what people think of him. What he can control is whether he gives them grounds, which is why verses 7–8 told him to be a model whose teaching offers no handle. A man is disregarded either because he has no authority or because he has given it away.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that the zeal for good works earns redemption. Redemption comes first, as Christ’s free gift; zeal for good works follows as its fruit. Nor does all authority mean Titus may be harsh or domineering; his authority is the authority of the message.

Did Christ die for everyone, or only for his people? This verse says he gave himself to redeem and purify a people for his own possession, and the purpose was achieved: they are redeemed and are being made zealous for good works. Reformed Christians therefore hold that Christ’s death was designed to save his elect and actually secures their salvation, rather than merely making salvation possible for all and certain for none (John 10:11, 15; Ephesians 5:25). Other evangelicals believe Christ died for every person in the same way. All agree that his death is of infinite worth, sufficient for the whole world, and that the gospel must be offered to everyone. What definite atonement adds is the certainty that the cross did not fail: everyone Christ died for will be his.

If I am not zealous for good works, am I really his? Zeal grows; it does not arrive full-grown. If you trust Christ and want to please him, even feebly, that desire is the beginning of what this verse describes. Ask God to stir it up, and feed it: think often about what Christ gave for you, because zeal is kindled by gratitude, not guilt. Spend time with believers who are eager to do good; zeal is contagious. Start small and practical. But if you feel no desire at all to please God, and are content to be so, take that seriously and go to Christ honestly about it. He does not reject the cold who come to him; he warms them.

In a sentence. Who gave himself up for us to set us free from every kind of wickedness and to make clean for himself a people who are his very own, eager to do what is good. Teach these things; encourage and correct with full authority. Do not let anyone look down on you.

On a Tuesday. Think of one good work you have been putting off, a visit, a gift, an apology, a kindness to a neighbour, and do it today, not to earn anything, but because you are his. And if you teach anyone, speak God’s word with the confidence it deserves, and live in a way that gives no one reason to disregard it.

For worship. Thank Christ that he gave himself for you, to redeem you and make you his own treasured possession. The great God paid the ransom with his own blood. He bought slaves out of the market of sin and made them a people for himself, a treasure he guards and delights in. He did not buy you to keep you at a distance. He purified you for himself. And he is making you, slowly and surely, into someone who burns with eagerness to do good, because that is what his love does to those it takes possession of.
verseByVerse.note: “A people for his own possession” echoes God’s words to Israel at Sinai.
