3.title: Heirs of Hope: Conduct in Society and the Gospel's Foundation
3.overview:
The last chapter covers life among unbelieving neighbours (vv. 1–8) and the handling of divisive people (vv. 9–15). Christians are to be good citizens, gentle and courteous to everyone, because they remember what they once were: foolish, enslaved and hateful. What changed them was not their own effort. God our Saviour appeared in kindness and saved us, “not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy”, by the new birth the Spirit gives, so that, justified by grace, we are heirs of eternal life.

Paul then tells Titus to insist on this free grace precisely so that believers will devote themselves to good works. Pointless controversies are to be avoided, a divisive person warned twice and then left alone, and the travelling teachers sent on well supplied.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — He Saved Us, Not Because of Works
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Believers are to respect the governing authorities, be ready to do good, speak evil of no one, avoid fighting, and show gentleness and courtesy to everyone. After all, we too were once foolish, disobedient and deceived, slaves to our desires, full of malice and envy, hating and hated. But when God our Saviour showed his kindness and love, he rescued us, not because of anything good we had done, but because of his mercy, by washing us through new birth and renewing us by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out generously through Jesus Christ. Justified by his grace, we have become heirs with the hope of eternal life. Paul wants Titus to stress this reliable truth, so that believers give themselves to doing good.
verseByVerse.theology:
Grace as the Engine of Works

Having excluded even our righteous works from the reason we are saved (v.5), Paul says to insist on that doctrine precisely so that believers devote themselves to good works (v.8). Free grace is not balanced against effort; it drives it.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: In a province prone to unrest, submission to authorities was the Christian's default posture (v.1; cf. Acts 5:29).

Now: Courtesy toward the ungodly comes from an accurate memory: ‘we ourselves were once’ (v.3).

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remind them to be submissive to rulers and authorities, to be obedient, to be ready for every good work, to speak evil of no one, to avoid quarreling, to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people.

Meaning first. Titus 3 moves from life within the church (chapter 2) to life in the wider world, and grounds both in the gospel. Believers are to be good citizens: submissive to authorities, ready to do good, never slandering, peaceable, gentle and courteous to everyone (vv. 1–2). Why? Because we were once no better than our pagan neighbours: foolish, disobedient, enslaved to passions, full of malice and hatred (v. 3). What changed us was not our own goodness but God’s: when his kindness and love appeared, he saved us, not because of righteous things we had done, but by his mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out on us through Christ, so that, justified by his grace, we became heirs of eternal life (vv. 4–7). This trustworthy saying must be stressed so that believers devote themselves to good works (v. 8). Titus must avoid foolish controversies and, after two warnings, have nothing more to do with a divisive person (vv. 9–11). The letter ends with travel plans, a call to help Zenas and Apollos, a last appeal for good works to meet urgent needs, and greetings and grace (vv. 12–15). At its centre stands one of the richest summaries of salvation in the Bible, in which Father, Son and Spirit all act to rescue people who hated one another.

Remind them. “Remind” (hypomimnēske) means keep reminding. It implies they had been told before, and that being told once is not enough. Much of a minister’s work is not new information but recollection, and much of the Christian life is remembering what we already know.

To be submissive to rulers and authorities. “Submissive” (hypotassesthai) means ordering themselves under. “Rulers and authorities” (archai exousiai) means civil government. It is the same political teaching as Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2: God has instituted government for order and justice (Romans 13:1–7; 1 Peter 2:13–17). And it needs its context. Crete was a Roman province with a reputation for unruliness and rebellion, and the churches contained Jewish converts from a background of resentment against Rome. A movement suspected of sedition would have been crushed. Believers must be different.

To be obedient. “Obedient” (peitharchein) means to obey those in authority, in all that does not require sin (Acts 5:29). It is not unqualified, and the New Testament never makes it so. The same apostles told a council they must obey God rather than men. Submission is the Christian’s default posture toward legitimate authority; it is not a promise to do whatever he is told.

To be ready for every good work. “Ready” (hetoimos) means prepared. There is the letter’s refrain again, and note where it sits. Good works are named here as a form of civic usefulness: not just avoiding trouble, but actively contributing to the common good of society (Jeremiah 29:7; Galatians 6:10). Christians are to be the people a town is glad to have in it.

To speak evil of no one. Then four things about speech and temper, and they are the most searching part of the passage. “Speak evil” (blasphēmein) means to slander, revile. Not even rulers, or pagan neighbours, or opponents. Christians are not to be known for abusive speech, even about those who oppose them.

To avoid quarrelling, to be gentle. “Avoid quarrelling” (amachos) is literally to be non-combatant, peaceable, the same requirement as for an overseer (1 Timothy 3:3). “Gentle” (epieikēs) is a word that resists translation: gracious, reasonable, yielding, the person who does not insist on the last inch of his rights.

And to show perfect courtesy toward all people. “Perfect courtesy” (pasan endeiknymenous prautēta) is literally showing all meekness, humility and consideration toward all people, and the doubled all is the point. Every kind of gentleness, toward every kind of person: not only fellow believers but every person, including unbelievers and enemies. On Crete that meant the liars and idle bellies of 1:12, the pagan neighbours, and the Roman officials. Christian kindness should be universal. That is a demanding standard and Paul knows exactly how demanding, which is why the next verse begins with for. He is about to explain how anybody could possibly treat such people that way.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Christians must obey government when it commands sin, or that they may never speak truthfully about injustice. The prophets and apostles did (Acts 4:19–20). It means our basic posture toward authority and neighbours is respect, peace and kindness, not contempt.

How should a Christian speak about politicians he disagrees with? Truthfully, but without contempt. You may say plainly that a policy is unjust, that a leader has lied, or that a law contradicts God’s word; the prophets did. But you may not mock, curse, spread rumours, or speak of anyone as though they were beneath respect. Pray for them by name, as Paul commands (1 Timothy 2:1–2). Before you post or repeat something, ask whether it is true, whether it is kind, and whether you would say it to their face. Paul wrote this under Nero. If courtesy was owed to him, it is owed to the people in office now, of every party.

When must a Christian refuse to obey the government? When it commands what God forbids, or forbids what God commands. The apostles refused to stop preaching (Acts 5:29); Daniel kept praying (Daniel 6:10); the Hebrew midwives refused to kill babies (Exodus 1:17). Even then, refuse respectfully and openly, accept the lawful penalty, and do not turn to violence or deceit. In free societies you may also use lawful means to change bad laws: voting, petitioning, speaking, standing for office. What you may not do is treat every law you dislike as an excuse to ignore authority altogether.

In a sentence. Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to obey them, and to be ready for every good deed; to speak badly of no one, to be peaceable and gracious, and to show complete gentleness to everyone.

On a Tuesday. How do you speak about political leaders and opponents, online and in person? Choose courtesy and gentleness this week. And look for one practical good work in your neighbourhood, something that would make your street or town glad there are Christians in it.

For worship. The King of kings is the gentlest of rulers. He did not cry aloud or lift up his voice in the street; a bruised reed he would not break. He stood before Pilate and did not revile him, submitted to unjust authority, and prayed for those who crucified him. All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him, and every earthly ruler holds office under his permission and will answer to him. That is why his people can be courteous to every ruler and every neighbour: the throne that matters is already occupied.

verseByVerse.quote: For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray, slaves to various passions and pleasures, passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another.

For we ourselves were once. There is the reason. The gentleness of verse 2 rests on the memory of verse 3. For gives the reason for gentleness toward all. Note the pronoun. Not they were, but we ourselves, and Paul includes himself. This is the Pharisee who was blameless in the righteousness of the law (Philippians 3:6) placing himself among the foolish and enslaved without qualification. “Once” (pote) means formerly. We have no reason to look down on unbelievers; we were exactly like them. Humility is the root of gentleness.

Foolish. Then seven items, and they trace a descent. “Foolish” (anoētoi) means without understanding, senseless: spiritually blind, unable to understand God’s truth (1 Corinthians 2:14; Ephesians 4:18).

Disobedient. “Disobedient” (apeitheis) means rebellious, refusing to be persuaded, the word from 1:16. Toward God, and often toward human authority.

Led astray. “Led astray” (planōmenoi) means deceived, wandering, and it is passive: we were deceived by sin and Satan. We did not only wander; we were led.

Slaves to various passions and pleasures. Then the condition it produced, and it is the honest word for it. “Slaves” (douleuontes) means serving as slaves. “Passions” (epithymiai) are desires; “pleasures” (hēdonai) is the word from which comes hedonism. Not indulging appetites but owned by them. We thought we were free, but we were enslaved to our desires (John 8:34; Romans 6:16–20).

Passing our days in malice and envy. “Malice” (kakia) means ill will, wickedness. “Envy” (phthonos) means jealousy. The phrase means spending our existence in it: not occasional lapses but the medium a life was lived in.

Hated by others and hating one another. And the last two are the worst. “Hated” (stygētoi) means detestable, odious. That final clause is the end of the descent. It describes a society, not only individuals: mutual hatred, everyone despising and being despised. A society without God becomes a web of mutual hatred. Anyone who has watched a community turn on itself knows the picture, and Paul says: that was us.

An accurate memory. Now put verses 2 and 3 together, because the logic is the heart of the letter. How do you show perfect courtesy to people who are foolish, enslaved and hateful? By remembering that the description is your own. This is Paul’s answer to the superiority a moral religion breeds, and it is the only answer that works. Contempt for the ungodly is not defeated by trying harder to be patient; it is defeated by an accurate memory. The Cretan liar is not a different species from the man teaching him. He is a man at a stage his teacher has been through, and the only thing that moved the teacher out of it is named in the very next verse.

What it does not mean. It does not mean every unbeliever is as bad as they could be in outward behaviour, or that no unbeliever does anything good in a civil sense. It means that, apart from grace, every part of human nature is corrupted by sin and unable to turn to God (Romans 3:10–18; 8:7–8). This is total inability: not that we are as wicked as possible, but that we cannot save ourselves.

If I was raised a Christian, does this describe me? Yes, though it may not feel like it. Paul was raised in the most careful religious home imaginable and still put himself in this list. You may never have been a drunkard or a thief, but the root of this verse is in every human heart: blindness to God, a will that resists him, desires that rule us, envy and pride. A respectable life can hide that from others and from ourselves. The point is not that you must invent a dramatic past, but that you must see your heart as God sees it, and know that you too were saved only by mercy. That is what will keep you gentle with people whose sins are louder than yours.

How do I stop feeling superior to unbelievers? Remember, regularly and specifically, what you were and what you still would be without grace. Remember that the difference between you and them was made by God, not by you (1 Corinthians 4:7). Get to know unbelievers as people, not as categories, and you will often find kindness, honesty and wisdom in them that rebuke you. Pray for them by name; it is very hard to despise someone you are praying for. And keep looking at the cross, where it becomes clear that Christ died for the ungodly, which includes you.

In a sentence. For there was a time when we too were senseless, rebellious and deceived, slaves to all kinds of cravings and pleasures, living in spite and jealousy, hateful and hating each other.

On a Tuesday. Think of the person whose behaviour most annoys or disgusts you, perhaps a neighbour, a public figure, a relative who does not believe. Then read this verse slowly and put your own name in it. Ask God to make you gentle toward them this week.

For worship. Remember what you were before Christ, and then look at what he did. He did not wait for the haters to become lovable. He came into a world that hated him and hated itself, and he loved it. He was hated without a cause so that hateful people could be loved without a cause. Every believer is a former slave of passions, a former hater, set free by the Son of God. Thank God for his grace, and let that memory make you gentle with those still lost.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit,
verseByVerse.commentary:
But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit,

But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Saviour appeared. But marks the great turning point, and it turns everything. Into the mutual hatred of verse 3, something appeared. “Goodness” (chrēstotēs) means kindness, generosity. “Loving kindness” (philanthrōpia) is literally love for humanity, and it is our word philanthropy. The Greeks praised rulers for their philanthropy; Paul says the true philanthropy is God’s. It is a startling term to use of God toward the people just described. He is not merely merciful to them; he is a lover of mankind. “Appeared” (epephanē) is the shining-out word, as in 2:11. God’s kindness appeared in Christ.

He saved us. “Saved” (esōsen) is aorist: a completed act. Past tense, decisive, done. God is the subject; we are the object. Salvation is God’s act, not our achievement.

Not because of works done by us in righteousness. Then Paul does what he always does and rules out the obvious misunderstanding before anyone can reach it. Notice how thorough the exclusion is. Not merely not because of works, but not because of works done by us in righteousness: even our righteous ones. The best things we ever did are excluded from the reason. Even our best deeds could not save us (Ephesians 2:8–9; Romans 3:20; 2 Timothy 1:9). This excludes all works, even religious ones, as the basis of salvation. And in a letter that mentions good works again and again, Paul makes certain nobody can misread their function.

But according to his own mercy. “Mercy” (eleos) is compassion for the helpless. The whole cause is on God’s side, and mercy is what is shown to the wretched rather than the deserving. The cause of salvation is in God, not in us.

By the washing of regeneration. Then the means. “Washing” (loutron) means bath, cleansing. “Regeneration” (palingenesia) means new birth, rebirth, literally genesis again: a new beginning, not a repaired old one. The word is used only here and in Matthew 19:28, of the renewal of the world. The new birth is a spiritual washing, a cleansing from sin, as promised in Ezekiel 36:25–27, where God promises to sprinkle clean water and give a new heart and a new spirit. It is the same new birth Jesus described to Nicodemus (John 3:3–8).

And renewal of the Holy Spirit. “Renewal” (anakainōsis) means making new again, renovation. The Holy Spirit is the agent of both the washing and the renewal. Probably one event is described two ways: the Spirit washes away sin’s defilement and creates new life. Regeneration is the beginning; renewal continues throughout life (Romans 12:2; 2 Corinthians 4:16). Both are the Spirit’s, and neither is ours.

Where Christians differ: does baptism regenerate? Roman Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and some Anglican traditions take the washing of regeneration to mean baptism, which in their view causes or conveys the new birth. Verdict: The washing is the Spirit’s inner cleansing, which baptism pictures but does not cause. Paul has just said salvation is not by works done by us; if a ritual performed by us caused regeneration, that would contradict it. The new birth is the Spirit’s sovereign work, like the wind (John 3:8), and it is received by faith (Galatians 3:26–27). Baptism is the outward sign of this inward washing, rightly given to those who profess faith. Scripture shows people regenerated before baptism (Acts 10:44–48) and baptised without being regenerated (Acts 8:13, 20–23).

Water and the Spirit. Those who read the verse as baptism also point to being born of water and the Spirit (John 3:5) and to Peter’s statement that baptism, which corresponds to the flood, now saves you (1 Peter 3:21). But Jesus was speaking to Nicodemus before Christian baptism existed, in the language of Ezekiel’s cleansing water and new spirit; and Peter immediately explains that he means not the removal of dirt from the body but an appeal to God for a good conscience, through the resurrection of Jesus Christ. The washing is the cleansing God performs, of which baptism is the sign. Our paedobaptist brothers in the Reformed tradition agree that the water does not itself regenerate, though they give the sign to the children of believers; we believe Scripture gives it to those who profess faith.

What it does not mean. It does not mean regeneration is a reward for faith. Regeneration is God’s work in the dead sinner, which produces faith (John 1:12–13; Ephesians 2:4–5). This is effectual calling: God gives life, and the sinner then believes.

If baptism does not save, why be baptised? Because Christ commands it (Matthew 28:19), and because it is the God-given sign of what he has done for you. In baptism you publicly confess your faith, picture your washing from sin, your death and resurrection with Christ (Romans 6:3–4), and your entry into his visible church. It does not make you a Christian, but a Christian who refuses it is disobeying his Lord. If you have trusted Christ and have not been baptised as a believer, speak to your pastor. It is not a reward for spiritual maturity; it is the first step of obedience for every new disciple.

How do I know I have been born again? Not by remembering the moment, which many believers cannot, but by its fruit. The new birth shows itself in faith in Christ, love for God and his people, a new attitude to sin, a desire for his word, and a life that is changing, however slowly (1 John 3:9–10, 14; 5:1). You did not cause it any more than you caused your first birth, but you can see that you are alive. If you trust Christ, you have been born again, because no one comes to Christ unless the Spirit has given him life. And if you are unsure, do not stare inward; look to Christ and ask him for life. He gives the Spirit to those who ask.

In a sentence. But when the kindness and love of God our Saviour for humanity appeared, he saved us, not because of any right things we had done, but because of his own mercy, by washing us through the new birth and making us new by the Holy Spirit.

On a Tuesday. Write down, in one sentence, why God saved you. If anything in the sentence is about you, cross it out and try again. Then spend a few minutes thanking him for mercy, and treat one difficult person today with the kindness God has shown you.

For worship. Thank God that your salvation rests on his mercy, not your merit. The lover of mankind looked on people who were hating one another and did not destroy them; he washed them. He did not patch up the old life; he gave a new birth. He did not wait for our righteous deeds; he set them all aside and saved us by mercy alone. You were washed and made new by the Spirit, and the God who began that new creation will finish it, when the regeneration of the whole world comes and all things are made new.

verseByVerse.quote: whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
whom he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

Whom he poured out on us richly. “Whom” is the Holy Spirit. “Poured out” (execheen) is the language of Pentecost: I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh (Joel 2:28; Acts 2:17, 33). What was promised to the prophets and given at Pentecost is here described as having happened to a scatter of Cretan believers. And “richly” (plousiōs) is worth stopping on: abundantly, lavishly. Not measured out, not rationed by merit or maturity. Poured, abundantly, on the people who were hating one another in verse 3. God does not ration the Spirit; every believer receives him in fullness (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13).

Through Jesus Christ our Saviour. The Spirit comes through Christ, who received him from the Father and poured him out (Acts 2:33; John 15:26). And there is the alternation again. God our Saviour in verse 4, Jesus Christ our Saviour here, two verses apart. After 2:13 we know it is not carelessness.

The whole Trinity. Note also that all three persons are at work in a single sentence: the Father’s kindness (v. 4), the Spirit’s renewal (v. 5), through Christ the Saviour (v. 6). Paul is not here expounding the Trinity; he is simply unable to describe salvation without all three of them.

So that being justified by his grace. Then the purpose. “Justified” (dikaiōthentes) means declared righteous. It is the courtroom word, the verdict pronounced: God, the Judge, declares sinners righteous in his sight, not because they are righteous in themselves, but because Christ’s righteousness is credited to them (Romans 3:21–26; 4:5; 2 Corinthians 5:21). “By his grace” means freely, as a gift, closing the door verse 5 had already shut. Justification is distinct from regeneration (God’s work in us), but always accompanies it. In the order of Paul’s thought: regeneration by the Spirit, justification by grace, and the hope of glory.

We might become heirs. “Heirs” (klēronomoi) are those who inherit. Justified sinners are adopted as God’s children and heirs, with Christ (Romans 8:17; Galatians 4:7). And this is the part most often missed. The sentence does not stop at the verdict. Justification is not the destination; it is what makes the inheritance possible. An acquitted man walks out of court owing nothing and owning nothing. Paul says we walk out as heirs, which is family language, not legal. The court declares us not guilty and the Father writes us into the will.

According to the hope of eternal life. Our inheritance is eternal life, already possessed in part, fully enjoyed in the future. It is the same hope named in the letter’s first sentence (1:2), promised before the ages began by the God who cannot lie. The letter has come round to where it started.

Where Christians differ: is justification a declaration, or a process of becoming righteous? Roman Catholic teaching holds that justification includes the infusion of righteousness, so that a person is made righteous over time and may grow in justification. Verdict: Justification is a once-for-all legal declaration by God that the believing sinner is righteous in his sight, on the basis of Christ’s righteousness imputed to him, received by faith alone. Our sins are counted to Christ, and his righteousness is counted to us (double imputation, 2 Corinthians 5:21). Sanctification, the process of being made holy, follows and is inseparable, but it is not the ground of our acceptance.

What it does not mean. It does not mean that justified people can live as they please. The very next verse insists on good works. But good works flow from justification; they are not its cause.

Why does it matter whether justification is a declaration or a process? Because it decides where your assurance rests. If you are justified by being made righteous over time, you can never be sure you are righteous enough, and your standing with God rises and falls with your performance. If you are justified by God’s declaration on the ground of Christ’s righteousness, your standing is as secure as Christ’s, complete from the moment you believe, and it cannot be improved or lost. That is not a licence to sin; it is the freedom to grow without fear. Sanctification is real and necessary, but you pursue it as a child already accepted, not as a defendant still awaiting the verdict.

What does it mean that the Spirit was poured out richly on me, when I feel so dry? It means he has been given to you in fullness, whatever you feel. Every believer has the Spirit (Romans 8:9); there is no second class of Christians who have more of him by right. Feelings rise and fall, and seasons of dryness come to the godliest believers, as the psalms show. But the Spirit is still at work in you, keeping you in faith, convicting you of sin, drawing you to Christ. Seek to be filled with the Spirit (Ephesians 5:18) by using the means he uses: the word, prayer, the Lord’s Supper and fellowship. Ask God for a fresh sense of his presence, and he will not give you a stone.

In a sentence. The Spirit whom he poured out on us in full measure through Jesus Christ our Saviour, so that, having been declared righteous by his grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life.

On a Tuesday. Say this to yourself today, especially when you feel condemned: I have been justified by his grace, and I am an heir of eternal life. Then live this day as an heir, not a beggar: generous, unafraid, and thankful.

For worship. Rejoice that you are justified, declared righteous by God for Christ’s sake, and that you are an heir of eternal life. The Father’s kindness planned it; the Son’s blood and righteousness secured it; the Spirit, poured out lavishly, applies it. The Judge has pronounced you not guilty, and the Father has written your name in his will beside his Son’s. Everything that belongs to Christ is yours by inheritance, and the God who cannot lie has promised it.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The saying is trustworthy, and I want you to insist on these things, so that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. These things are excellent and profitable for people.

The saying is trustworthy. The fifth and last of the trustworthy sayings in these letters (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11). Here it points backwards, to the great statement of verses 4–7, perhaps an early creed or hymn about salvation.

And I want you to insist on these things. “Insist” (diabebaiousthai) means to speak confidently, to affirm strongly, to maintain. It is the same word used of the false teachers’ confident assertions (1 Timothy 1:7). Titus is to be confident about the right things. He is not merely to mention this doctrine but to press it.

So that those who have believed in God may be careful to devote themselves to good works. Then the purpose, and it is the sentence that holds the whole letter together. Read the logic carefully, because it runs the opposite way from what most people expect. Paul has just excluded works from salvation as thoroughly as language allows. And now he says: insist on that doctrine, so that people will do good works. The free grace is not a concession that has to be balanced by a warning about effort. It is the engine of the effort. Paul’s method for producing a hard-working church is to press justification by grace alone, which is exactly what he said in 2:11–12, where grace itself is the schoolmaster. Grace does not lead to laziness; it is the only true motive for goodness.

Careful and devoted. “Be careful” (phrontizōsin) means to think about, give attention to, apply the mind: good works are to be planned rather than left to chance. “Devote themselves” (proistasthai) is a strong word for taking the lead in something, practising it, being occupied with it, sometimes used of practising a trade; it is the same word used for elders who manage or lead (1 Timothy 3:4; 5:17). Believers should take the lead in good works. Christians are to be in the business of it.

These things are excellent and profitable for people. “Excellent” (kala) means good, fine. “Profitable” (ōphelima) means useful, beneficial. It is the plainest possible commendation. Sound doctrine and good works benefit people, both believers and the wider society. And it stands against the verdict on the alternative in the very next verse, where controversies are unprofitable. Paul is holding up two ways a church can spend its energy and pricing them both.

What it does not mean. It does not mean good works earn salvation. Verses 5–7 have just excluded that. Good works are the fruit and evidence of saving faith (Ephesians 2:10; James 2:17–18).

If I am saved by grace alone, why should I work so hard at good works? Because grace has made you a child of God, and children love to please their Father. Because Christ gave himself to make you zealous for good works (2:14), and to neglect them is to neglect the very thing he died for. Because they glorify God and bring others to him (Matthew 5:16). Because they bless people who need them. And because they are the evidence, to yourself and others, that your faith is real. You do not work for your salvation; you work from it, with the energy of someone who has nothing to prove and everything to give.

In a sentence. This is a reliable saying, and I want you to stress these truths confidently, so that those who have put their trust in God will take care to devote themselves to doing good. These things are excellent and benefit everyone.

On a Tuesday. What good work could you take the lead in this week, in your church, workplace or neighbourhood? Do not wait to be asked. Plan it, as Paul says: be careful to devote yourself to it. Write it in your diary.

For worship. The God who saved us by mercy alone did not save us to be idle. He re-created us in Christ Jesus for good works, which he prepared beforehand for us to walk in. Our good works are not the price of his love but its overflow, and even they are his gift. And on the last day he will commend what his own grace produced in us, saying well done to servants who did nothing but receive. That is the generosity of the God who saves.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Titus should keep away from pointless arguments about genealogies and disputes about the law, which achieve nothing. Someone who causes divisions should be warned twice and then avoided, since he has turned aside and condemns himself. Paul arranges to meet Titus at Nicopolis for the winter once a replacement arrives, asks him to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey, and reminds him that believers must learn to give themselves to good works that meet urgent needs and bear fruit. He closes with greetings and grace.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Divisive Man, and the Limit on Patience

The factious man (hairetikos) is warned twice, and then left (v.10): restraint and an end, both. Having been told plainly, he stands self-condemned (v.11).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Controversies are ‘unprofitable’ (v.9), set against good works that are ‘profitable’ (v.8).

Now: The letter's refrain lands on something small: see that two travellers lack nothing (vv.13–14).

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless. As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him, knowing that such a person is warped and sinful; he is self-condemned.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, dissensions, and quarrels about the law, for they are unprofitable and worthless. As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him, knowing that such a person is warped and sinful; he is self-condemned.

But avoid foolish controversies. “Avoid” (periistaso) means stand clear of, shun, as in 2 Timothy 2:16. The instruction is to shun them, not to win them. “Foolish controversies” (mōrai zētēseis) are stupid speculative questions, as in 2 Timothy 2:23.

Genealogies. As in 1 Timothy 1:4: speculations built on Old Testament family trees, the same list as at Ephesus.

Dissensions, and quarrels about the law. “Dissensions” (eris) means strife, rivalry. “Quarrels about the law” (machai nomikai) are legal battles, fights over the law of Moses: the circumcision party’s debates about Jewish rules (1:10, 14).

For they are unprofitable and worthless. “Unprofitable” (anōpheleis) means useless, in deliberate contrast with profitable (v. 8). “Worthless” (mataioi) means empty, futile. The verdict is commercial. Set against verse 8’s excellent and profitable, Paul is running a ledger. A church has a fixed amount of energy, and every hour spent on quarrels about the law is an hour not spent on cases of urgent need (v. 14). The argument is not that controversy is unpleasant but that it produces nothing.

As for a person who stirs up division. Then verses 10–11, which give the New Testament’s most concrete procedure for a particular kind of person. “Stirs up division” (hairetikos) means factious, divisive, party-making, and it is the word from which we get heretic. But at this date it means a divisive person, one who forms factions around his own opinions and splits the church. In later church usage, heretic came to mean one who teaches serious doctrinal error. The offence named here is not primarily wrong belief but the splitting of a congregation.

After warning him once and then twice. “Warning” (nouthesia) means admonition, counsel. Patience and due process: two warnings give a chance to repent (Matthew 18:15–17). And notice the restraint built into the procedure. Not once, but twice. The man is to be warned, and then warned again, before anything else happens. Paul is not licensing a quick trigger, and a church that removes someone without clear warnings has not followed this text.

Have nothing more to do with him. “Have nothing to do with” (paraitou) means refuse, reject, avoid: stop engaging and exclude him from fellowship. Further argument only feeds his divisiveness. But notice equally that the process ends. Have nothing more to do with him is decisive, and there is no third warning. Endless patience with a man who is dividing a church is not kindness to the church, and Paul sets a limit.

Knowing that such a person is warped and sinful. “Warped” (exestraptai) means turned inside out, perverted, twisted. “Sinful” (hamartanei) is present tense: he keeps on sinning.

He is self-condemned. “Self-condemned” (autokatakritos) means condemned by himself, and it is the striking word. He passes sentence on himself. The two warnings are what make it so: a man who has been told twice, plainly, and persists, has convicted himself out of his own mouth. The church merely recognises it. Titus does not have to judge him. He only has to notice.

What it does not mean. It does not mean anyone who disagrees with church leaders should be excluded. The issue is a divisive spirit that splits the church over foolish and unprofitable matters and refuses correction. Nor does it mean believers should avoid all discussion of hard questions; serious theological study is good.

How do I tell a foolish controversy from a necessary one? Ask whether Scripture speaks clearly to it and whether it touches the gospel or godliness. Titus must rebuke false teachers sharply (1:13) and refute those who contradict sound doctrine (1:9), so defending the truth is not optional. What Paul forbids are arguments built on speculation, things Scripture does not settle, debates pursued for the pleasure of winning, and quarrels that feed curiosity and pride rather than faith and love. A useful test: is this debate making anyone more like Christ, or only more certain they are right? Online, the answer is usually obvious.

What does have nothing more to do with him mean in practice? After two warnings, the church is to put him out of its fellowship, as Jesus and Paul teach elsewhere (Matthew 18:15–17; 1 Corinthians 5:11–13). He should not be allowed to teach, lead or keep spreading division within the church. Believers should not keep debating with him or giving him an audience. But the aim is still repentance: do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Be courteous if you meet him, pray for him, and be ready to welcome him back gladly if he repents. The divisive person is one who will not stop stirring up quarrels, not someone who disagrees honestly.

In a sentence. But steer clear of foolish disputes, genealogies, arguments and fights about the law, because they are useless and empty. As for someone who causes divisions, warn him once and then a second time, and after that have nothing more to do with him. You can be sure that such a person is twisted and keeps on sinning; he has condemned himself.

On a Tuesday. Are you contributing to unity or division in your church? If you have a grievance, take it to the person, not to a faction. And notice which arguments you are drawn into this week, online and in person. If one is unprofitable, step out of it.

For worship. Christ prayed that his people would be one, as he and the Father are one, and he died to break down the dividing walls between them. He hates what divides his body, because he gave his own body to make it one. And he is patient: he warns before he judges, and he receives every wanderer who returns. The church is not held together by winning arguments but by the Lord who holds it, and the gates of hell, let alone a divisive man, will not prevail against it.

verseByVerse.quote: When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way; see that they lack nothing. And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to come to me at Nicopolis, for I have decided to spend the winter there. Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way; see that they lack nothing. And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works, so as to help cases of urgent need, and not be unfruitful.

When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you. Practical arrangements, and even here the letter’s themes keep surfacing. Artemas appears nowhere else in Scripture. Tychicus we know: the courier of Ephesians and Colossians, the beloved brother and faithful minister (Ephesians 6:21; Colossians 4:7; 2 Timothy 4:12). One of the two will replace Titus in Crete, so that the churches would not be left without leadership. Paul does not pull a man out of a post without putting someone in it.

Do your best to come to me at Nicopolis. Nicopolis, city of victory, was probably the city of that name on the west coast of Greece, in Epirus, founded by Augustus to commemorate his victory at Actium. It was a good base for winter and for mission into Dalmatia, where Titus later went (2 Timothy 4:10).

For I have decided to spend the winter there. Paul is planning a season’s work and wants Titus with him, which incidentally tells us this letter was written when he was still free, between his imprisonments, before the chains of 2 Timothy.

Do your best to speed Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their way. Zenas the lawyer (nomikos) was either a Jewish expert in the law of Moses or a Roman jurist; he is otherwise unknown. Apollos was the eloquent teacher from Alexandria, mighty in the Scriptures, whom Priscilla and Aquila took aside to explain the way of God more accurately (Acts 18:24–28; 1 Corinthians 3:5–6). They were probably carrying this letter. “Speed on their way” (propempson) means to send forward, help on their journey: a technical term for providing missionaries with food, money and travel needs (Romans 15:24; 3 John 6).

See that they lack nothing. A practical instruction with a principle inside it. Travelling teachers depended entirely on the hospitality of churches, and a congregation that sent them off short had failed them. Generous support for travelling gospel workers was a Christian duty. Paul is specific about it in a letter he could have ended three verses earlier.

And let our people learn to devote themselves to good works. Then verse 14, which turns the errand into a lesson. “Our people” (hoi hēmeteroi) are the Cretan believers. Learn: good works do not come naturally; they must be learned, practised and cultivated. “Devote themselves” (proistasthai) is the same word as in verse 8.

So as to help cases of urgent need. “Urgent need” (anankaiai chreiai) means necessary needs, pressing necessities: not general benevolence but the specific emergency in front of you, of which Zenas and Apollos passing through is the immediate example, along with the poor and needy. The Cretans, known as idle bellies (1:12), must become known for working and giving.

And not be unfruitful. “Unfruitful” (akarpoi) means without fruit, and it is agricultural. A tree that produces nothing is not neutral; it is a failure at being a tree. A faith that produces no fruit is dead (Matthew 7:17–20; John 15:2, 8). So the letter’s great refrain lands, at the end, on something small and concrete: make sure two travellers have what they need for the journey. That is what devotion to good works looked like on Crete that week.

What it does not mean. It does not mean fruitfulness is measured only by visible results. It is the overflow of a life devoted to Christ.

How do I learn to devote myself to good works? The way you learn any skill: by practice, by example, and by planning. Watch believers who are good at it and copy them. Look at your week and ask where the urgent needs are: the neighbour after surgery, the family short of money, the missionary on furlough, the student far from home. Set aside money and time in advance, so you are ready when the need arises. Start with what is in front of you rather than waiting for a grand opportunity. And do it as worship, remembering that whatever you do for the least of Christ’s brothers you do for him (Matthew 25:40).

How should my church care for missionaries and visiting preachers? Generously and thoughtfully, so that they lack nothing. Pay their expenses and give a proper gift, not a token. Offer hospitality: a bed, meals, a car, a quiet place to rest. Ask what they actually need, and listen. Pray for them by name, and keep in touch after they leave. Support missionaries over the long term, not only when they visit. John says we ought to support people like these, that we may be fellow workers for the truth (3 John 8). A church that sends its gospel workers on their way well shares in their reward.

In a sentence. When I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, do your best to join me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to spend the winter there. Do everything you can to help Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey, and make sure they have everything they need. Our people must learn to give themselves to doing good, so that they can meet urgent needs and not live unproductive lives.

On a Tuesday. Support a missionary or gospel worker this week, with a gift, a letter or prayer. See that they lack nothing. And identify one urgent need near you, in your church or street, and meet it before Sunday.

For worship. The Lord of the harvest sends out his workers and sees that they lack nothing; he provided for Paul through the Philippians, for Apollos through Titus, and for his servants still through his people’s generosity. He himself came as a traveller with nowhere to lay his head, dependent on the hospitality of others, and he counts every cup of water given to his servants as given to him. He is the true vine, and every fruitful life is his life flowing through a branch. Thank him for every good work he has prepared for you to walk in.

verseByVerse.quote: All who are with me send greetings to you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.
verseByVerse.commentary:
All who are with me send greetings to you. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.

All who are with me send greetings to you. No names, unusually; Paul often lists them. Whoever they were, they are anonymous here. But Paul was not alone at this time; he had a team.

Greet those who love us in the faith. “Love us in the faith” (tous philountas hēmas en pistei): those who share the faith and love Paul’s team. It is a warm and slightly wistful phrase. The letter has been full of people who did not: the insubordinate, the empty talkers, the men teaching for shameful gain, the divisive man to be warned twice. At the end Paul sends his greeting past all of them to the ones who love him, and the qualifier in the faith marks the bond: not personal affection merely, but the love of people who hold the same thing. Perhaps it is a gentle distinction from the false teachers.

Grace be with you all. Then the last words. “You all” (pantōn hymōn) is plural, as at the close of both letters to Timothy: the whole church of Crete. This letter has been addressed to one man on an island, full of instructions about how he should handle elders and false teachers and older women and slaves, and Paul knew perfectly well it would be read aloud to the congregations. So the last word goes to the room: to the elders being appointed, the older women told not to gossip, the young wives, the slaves not pilfering, and even, one supposes, the divisive man who still had two warnings coming.

The first word and the last. A letter full of instructions about good works ends, as it began (1:4), with grace. And grace is the letter’s argument as well as its frame. The grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people, training us (2:11–12); he saved us not because of works but according to his own mercy, so that being justified by his grace we might become heirs (3:5–7). Everything rests on grace.

What it does not mean. It does not mean grace is a polite closing formula. It is the most important thing Paul could wish for them.

Why does Paul end every letter with grace? Because grace is not only how the Christian life begins but how it continues and how it ends. We are saved by grace, trained by grace, kept by grace, and will be brought home by grace. Every instruction in this letter, to elders, older women, young men, slaves, citizens, assumes it; none of it can be obeyed without it. When Paul says grace be with you all, he is not adding a pleasant sign-off. He is naming the one thing that makes everything else possible, and handing them back to the God who supplies it.

In a sentence. Everyone with me sends you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with you all.

On a Tuesday. Thank God for those who love you in the faith, and tell one of them this week. And when you close a letter, a message or a conversation with a fellow believer, mean it when you wish them grace.

For worship. To an island proverbial for lying, gluttony and disorder, Paul sent a short letter about appointing decent men, telling people to behave, and grace. He seems to have thought that would be enough, and he was right, because the grace he wished them was not his own. It is the grace of the God who never lies, who promised eternal life before the ages began, who appeared in the person of his Son to redeem a people for himself, and who poured out his Spirit richly on people who had hated one another. Pray for grace for your whole church today. It is with you all.
